subtopic: POST OFFICE
POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON ALLEGED CONFLICT OF INTEREST IN AWARDING OF CONTRACT TO ITT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allegations of conflict of interest have been made in this House and in the media after the Canada Post Office awarded a maximum 70 million dollar contract to ITT Canada for the manufacturing of mechanized letter sorting equipment.
Innuendos have been made concerning the integrity of two of my senior officers, Mr. John Mackay and Mr. Jack Moody.
Mr. John Mackay joined the Canada Post Office on October 6, 1969, as General Manager for our Ontario postal region. This appointment came after an extensive recruiting campaign in private industry by the Canada Post Office to attract highly competent people for its reorganization and decentralization program.
Though it is correct that Mr. Mackay was then president of ITT Canada Limited, this did not mean that we should have turned down his appointment just in case at one time or another his former employer might do business with the federal Government, let alone the Canada Post Office.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to state emphatically that Mr. Mackay has no more ties, financial interests or otherwise with ITT since he joined the Canada Post Office in 1969.
On October 21, 1960, Mr. Jack Moody came to the Canada Post Office from the Armed Forces as a metalur-gical engineer. He was assigned to our Engineering Branch and in 1971 became its chief engineer.
On April 17, 1968, Mr. Moody registered with the Career Assignment Program (CAP) administered by the Public Service Commission. His application was approved by the Assistant Deputy Postmaster General-Personnel on June 8, 1970. It was then accepted by the Public Service Commission. From January to March 1971, Mr. Moody left the department to follow the theoretical part of the Career Assignment Program as required.
Unfortunately, the Public Service Commission was unable to find a suitable assignment for Mr. Moody after his three month course. This was mostly because of Mr. Moody's high classification and salary range. This is why the Canada Post Office decided in July 1971, with the agreement of Treasury Board and the Public Service Commission, responsible for CAP, to put Mr. Moody on a Developmental Program. On this basis, Mr. Moody was assigned to ITT Canada for a period not exceeding two years starting September 1st 1971 with the view of broadening his knowledge. Upon his return to Ottawa, the department will benefit from the services of a qualified civil servant who will be competent in the installation, operation and utilization of automatic letter sorting machines.
In keeping with the terms and conditions of this program, Mr. Moody is still a public service employee and is paid by the Government of Canada. ITT Canada reimburses all expenditures-wages and incidentals-to the Receiver General of Canada. In similar programs, we have another Post Office employee on assignment with Imperial Oil. Furthermore, we have had employees from Gulf Oil and Bell Canada working with the Canada Post Office on assignment. We do not have any other Post Office employee working on coding and mechanization with companies other than ITT Canada for the simple reason that it is the pnly one which entered this field with a manufacturing plant in Canada.
The Canada Post Office has not had any active research and development program in recent years in the mechanization field. It has simply studied, supplemented by published documentation, different pieces of mechanized equipment now in use and queried other postal authorities on their performance and expectations regarding their particular coding and mechanization programs. This is the responsibility of our Coding and Mechanization Branch. To be specific it is the main responsibility of Mr. Jerry Fultz. Mr. Moody never worked for our Coding and Mechanization Branch nor did he in any way collaborate

March 6, 1972
ITT Contract Award
in its work. As for Mr. Gerry Fultz, he joined the Canada Post Office on February 12, 1940. Since then he has had vast experience in the Department particularly in the operations and administration field. Mr. Fultz was named Director of the new Coding and Mechanization Branch on June 16, 1970.
On November 24, 1970, Mr. Fultz recommended that the Post Office call for tenders for automatic letter sorting equipment needed for the mechanization of the Ottawa Post Office. Twenty-seven companies which we knew manufactured such equipment were invited to submit tenders. Tenders closed January 12, 1971.
A specifications book was given to the interested parties. It was understood that the equipment was to be delivered in two stages. We knew very well that the first stage could not be built in Canada. But we specified definitely that the second stage of the contract had to be Canadian-built.
We received five bids: ITT Canada on behalf of ITT Belgium; Canadian Marconi on behalf of GEC Elliott of Great Britain; Telefunken; Plessey Canada on behalf of Plessey of Great Britain; and Plessey Canada on behalf of Plessey of Great Britain-Plessey of Australia and Toshiba.
Technical appraisals determined that the equipment proposed by Telefunken and that of ITT Canada were the best on the grounds of proven standard quality. Hence, because of costs, shipment dates and the ability to produce in Canada, the ITT Canada tender was judged to be superior. Therefore I sent a submission to Treasury Board recommending approval of the ITT Canada bid. It was approved by Treasury Board after being studied by the Department of Supply and Services and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Thus, on March 30, 1971, a $4.4 million contract was awarded to ITT Canada.
The equipment corresponding to the first stage of the contract has recently arrived at the Ottawa Post Office from Belgium. ITT Canada has already started the manufacturing process, in Canada, of the second stage.
In September 1971, ITT Canada informed the Canada Post Office verbally that it was ready to provide automatic letter sorting machines which the department needed for the other 14 Canadian centres at the same unit base price. Though I could have legally and technically recommended to Treasury Board the awarding of the contract to ITT Canada on the basis of its first bid, I asked my officials to call for another tender. My purpose was to give other companies another chance and also to see if we could get a better deal.
Tenders were called October 6, 1971 and again a specifications book was sent to the interested parties. Fourteen companies in five countries were invited to submit bids. Tenders closed November 18, 1971. Only two bids were received: Plessey Canada for Plessey-GEC Elliott of Great Britain, and ITT Canada.
Technically and legally, the department could have ignored the Plessey Canada bid. In fact that bid did not

meet the specifications of the tender call in many instances. Nevertheless, I asked Mr. Fultz to study thoroughly the Plessey Canada bid and to contact them to ask for extensive amplification, clarification and new data regarding the bid.
An evaluation of the two bids was finished by the end of January, 1972. On February 1, 1972, at the request of the British High Commissioner in Ottawa who was making a representation to us on behalf of Plessey of Great Britain, I agreed not to make a decision on the matter and to delay my recommendation to Treasury Board until Mr. Fultz met again with top executives of Plessey of Great Britain to hear their new arguments on the proposed equipment. On the same day, Mr. Fultz left for England for the fifth time in two years. He went to examine again the present status of the equipment of Plessey of Great Britain.
Following his return from England Mr. Fultz reported that, while he had seen equipment being developed which had capabilities for fulfilling the specifications should it be placed in production, as yet none of it was in the production stage. And a fair amount of development work remained to be done before it could be fully assessed. After his report, I sent my submission forward to Treasury Board recommending the contract be awarded to ITT Canada. My proposal was accepted by Treasury Board.
The reasons for my recommendations and Treasury Board's decision are as follows:
1.	The ITT Canada equipment is of the sixth generation of equipment which has successfully been in operation in many countries such as Belgium, the United States, the Federal Republic of Germany and Denmark. The proposed Plessey equipment is still in the research and development stages without even a prototype being assembled.
2.	While the ITT Canada equipment can handle 21,000 letters per hour regardless of size, the performance of the Plessey equipment, according to its own appraisal, ranges from 20,800 letters, 5| inches long, per hour to 14,100 letters, 10 inches long, per hour. These are the figures "throughput" by the machine. Throughput is maximum speed adjusted to allow for mail feed, stoppages, operator error, etc. and is the number of letters we can expect to get out of a machine in one hour of operation.
The majority of letter sizes for the government is more than eight inches in length. Thus the Plessey equipment would have allowed handling of 6,000 letters less per hour than the ITT Canada equipment.
3.	If we take into account that the average size of letters mailed in Canada is at least eight inches, it would have meant a purchase of 85 automatic letter sorting machines from Plessey while only 67 ITT Canada automatic letter sorting machines would have done the same work. Thus, if we had opted for the Plessey system, though the cost per machine would have been less it would have cost the Canada Post Office, over a 15-year period, 28 million extra budget dollars because of an increased demand for supplies and labour. Evidently with an increasing volume of mail over the years, the Plessey system would continue to cost the Post Office more money because of the ever-increasing number of machines needed.
March 6, 1972

Those three reasons should have been enough to justify awarding the contract to ITT Canada, but other reasons of equal importance moulded our decision. Let me just mention:
1.	Space needed: If we would have opted for the Plessey system, we would have been forced, because of the number of machines, to build bigger offices. Just to cite Montreal as an example, construction costs of our new proposed facilities would have been nearly $2 million more than forecasted.
2.	Canadian content: While ITT Canada guaranteed that the equipment in this contract would be built in Canada, the first seven automatic letter sorting machines and 72 coding desks of the Plessey system would have been built in England. To summarize, the ITT Canada proposal will create directly about 150 jobs in Canada this year while Plessey could not really do it before 1973.
I could also mention, Mr. Speaker, the advantages of the ITT Canada bid on future costs, on research, and the development in Canada of such an industry and its potential for export in harmony with existing government policy.
Nevertheless, I think I have proven beyond any doubt that the award of the contract to ITT Canada was in the best interest of the Canada Post Office and the Canadian people. I would have preferred, out of courtesy for Plessey, not to go into details, but circumstances forced me to do so. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that, as you are now aware of the fact that I was extremely cautious in connection with these bids, you will admit in all fairness that I went further than the usual tendering procedures.
But mostly, and more importantly, I hope that any doubts cast on the integrity of Mr. John Mackay and Mr. Jack Moody have been proven baseless and uncalled for.
These two senior public service employees have had no say whatsoever in the decision taken on this matter. I, alone, have made the decision after carefully studying the well-documented information and the recommendations which Mr. Fultz made to me. On this basis I then recommended to Treasury Board the award of the contract to ITT Canada knowing very well that my Deputy Postmaster General, John Mackay, had been president of that company and that Mr. Jack Moody was on assignment from the department to that same company.
I wish to thank you, Mr. Speaker, in the name of these two senior officials of my department, for your patience.

speechtext:
In fact, as I listened to the minister I almost thought he protested too much. This problem does raise
ITT Contract Award
some very basic questions. I quite agree with the minister it is unfortunate that men on the periphery are sometimes caught in the crossfire. However, until the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government define a code of ethics to remove any potential stain of conflict of interest in the discharge of legislature and administrative duties, these problems are going to return to haunt all members and to take the time of this chamber.
It was only in the bright days of 1968, which are now somewhat dulled and certainly distant, that the new Prime Minister and the new government were going to proclaim, at long last, a code of ethics. I have not got all the quotations here and I will not take up the time of the House, but I know that at that time the Prime Minister said on one occasion that conflicts of interest must be avoided and they were going to search for some kind of guidelines. Mr. Speaker, they have searched for guidelines almost like the biblical characters of old, wandering and stumbling through the wilderness. I am told that two reports even got to the Privy Council office recommending certain terms of reference to take care of this problem, and still there is no action.
Let no criticism from this side of the House unfortunately fall on those who are caught in this crossfire. We do need a code of ethics to define rules of conduct and to remove any possibility of conflict of interest for parliamentarians, be they in the House of Commons or the Senate, and certainly for some of the top administrators .in government.
In this case we have a deputy minister who was a former head to ITT, the chief engineer of the Post Office now seconded or leased or lent to ITT, and we have a contract for $70 million nine-tenths of the feet, which is not just a foot in the door but both feet in the door, for future contracts for the mechanization of the Post Office and postal services. This is a large item of government business.
Last Friday the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) cast innuendoes about tendering. It does not take much of a layman to know that with a detailed definition of specifications you can chart and determine the type of tender you want. It does not excite me that 27 companies applied initially although it is interesting that only five were interested in the specifications book. On we went from there.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the continual growth of the public and private sectors and the interrelationship of the government with the private sector demand a code of ethics. I believe there should be cross-fertilization and an infusion of new blood from the private into the public sector so that the public will have an appreciation of what motivates the private sector. I think we have to do more of that. I commend the minister for trying to experiment on that basis. But this interrelationship cannot be allowed to develop so that it in effect becomes incest between government and the private sector. I suggest, on the face of the matter and on the initial facts, that until the minister stood in his place today and gave a very detailed statement there were naturally questions that arose.
I shall not say much more. I think the whole problem of ITT could and very well may develop further questions in the not too distant future. This is not the first advent of ITT in government business. A company called Raynier

March 6, 1972
ITT Contract Award
Pulp and Paper, which is interested in pulp and paper rights in Canada, I am informed has received federal funds. Some of the timing of the federal commitment for federal funds might be involved in postal problems, but when we have a conglomerate like ITT and see the problems they have south of the border I think we have to ask questions.
To avoid these matters coming up on a recurring basis it is not the minister's but the government's responsibility to define a code of ethics so that parliamentarians in the Senate and in the House and also top administrators will be able to discharge their duties without getting caught in this type of crossfire. I believe we should have a committee to look into this matter. There should be terms of disclosure of personal interest in any legislative or administrative acts. We should come at least as far as Britain has come, let alone the United States, and define very carefully a code of ethics so this will not happen again.

subtopic: POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON ALLEGED CONFLICT OF INTEREST IN AWARDING OF CONTRACT TO ITT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister has perhaps misconceived the problem. The problem is not the integrity of public servants. I and my colleagues certainly do not question the integrity of Mr. Mackay and Mr. Moody who I am sure are very decent Canadians trying to do a job as they see it. I think the long explanation the minister gave in order to try to clear these two men of any suggestion of improper action may have been necessary in his own mind, but that is not the point at all. The point is that the entire situation is such as to create doubt about what is happening in the department and in other departments. The point is that if you are going to do business with ITT it is wrong to have as deputy minister an ex-president of ITT. The point is that if the government is going to do a large business with ITT it is wrong to have a senior official of the department seconded to ITT. These are the issues.
If the minister or the government tells me this is the only source for the equipment or the only company to which to send someone I tell them that they are downgrading Canada a great deal too much. There are other areas where these people could go and there are other firms where they could be trained. This cosy connection between the government and ITT of having a senior official there at the time the specification books arrive, when the specification books have to be studied, when the tender has to be made, this coincidence of a senior official of the department being there at that time seconded to the company-that is the kind of thing that creates problems and creates conflict of interest. No detailed statement about duties and all that will wash away the fact that there is a conflict of interest.
Anyone who has studied our society has long ago abandoned the notion that the company and the deputy minister or somebody from the department sit down in a smoke-filled room and cook up something. That is not the way it is done. It is done at luncheons. It is done at cocktail parties. It is done at dinners. It is done on the golf course and it is done in the boathouse. It is that kind of association that throws doubt on what is being done. Precisely because a government department is involved and tens of millions of dollars of the money of Canadian taxpayers, action must never be undertaken in a way

which may even remotely suggest the kind of thing that this action now suggests.
The hon. member who preceded me referred to ITT Rayonier in Quebec which has been offered $13.7 million by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I think of the fact that there are two members of the minister's advisory board who are officers of companies which have been offered grants of over $7 million. I think of the remission by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the previous Minister of Finance of $6 million to Great Canadian Oil Sands Limited, a subsidiary of Sun Oil in Alberta-a $6 million Christmas gift, I think of the statement of one of the spokesman for the Liberal party in Ontario to the effect that 95 corporations finance the activities of the government party between elections and at election time, and I say I am thoroughly justified in suggesting that the cosiness between the government and corporations such as ITT is a disservice to Canada and a disgrace to the democratic system. This is what disturbs me.
Despite the detailed and elaborate statement the minister has made I want to express the hope that the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications which will be studying the department's estimates will not be satisfied with the details that the minister gave. He has referred to a number of documents and you, Sir, ruled the other day that documents which are quoted or to which reference is made should be laid on the table. I hope that when the committee discusses the department's estimates it will demand that the minister lay on the table the submission to Treasury Board, the studies carried out by the two departments to which he referred, the Department of Supply and Services and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the actual contract with ITT, the specification books for the two orders, Mr. Fultz's report on the Plessey equipment, and the tenders submitted by all bidders. We have to see all these documents in order to make certain that the specifications were not tailored to ITT possibilities.

Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I would like to move a motion on a matter of pressing necessity. I ask for the consent of the House to propose a motion without notice in this regard. The urgency and the pressing nature of this matter concern the reasonable possibility of a cessation of postal services in Canada in the very near future. We are told that talks are now going on between Treasury Board and the postal unions, but the President of the Treasury Board has admitted that the board has not made a proposal on the essential issues of wages and job security guarantees. In the public interest there is urgency and a necessity that Treasury Board negotiate in good faith. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That this House instructs the President of the Treasury Board to report to the House on the status of the bargaining and the

proposals made by the Treasury Board to the postal unions on Tuesday and on each succeeding Tuesday until a collective agreement is signed.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, financing and guarantee bills, including the present one, have been introduced annually with the exception of the 1963 bill which covered 1962 and 1963, and the 1966 bill which covered 1965 and 1966. The present bill is basically the same as in previous years. It sets out, in summary form, the amounts of CNR's capital expenditures for 1971 as presented in its capital budget for that year totalling $219,800,000. This level of expenditures compares with $229,000,000 authorized in 1970. The bill also states that Canadian National Railways is authorized to make expenditures not exceeding $83,000,000 between January 1 and July 1, 1972 for obligations incurred prior to January 1, 1972 and to enter into contracts before July 1, 1972 for capital expenditures not exceeding $162,000,000 for which payment will not come due until after 1971.
The bill is intended to achieve six main objectives most of which have had similar expression in previous financing and guarantee bills.
First, the bill contains provisions authorizing Canadian National Railways to borrow up to $27,000,000 for financing branch line construction. This amount includes the financing of branch lines in excess of 20 miles authorized by special statute as well as the financing of those lines under 20 miles which do not require special legislation. By covering all branch lines, the provision in the bill is consistent with the intent of reflecting in the financing and guarantee bill all the financing authorities which Canadian National Railways require.
Second, the bill provides for the continued purchase by the Minister of Finance of Canadian National Railways' 4 per cent preferred stock through to the end of the calendar year 1972. This continues the practice of previous financing and guarantee acts. The 1970 Financing and Guarantee Act extended to December 31, 1971 the expiry date of the authority granted by the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act of 1952 for the purchase of such stock equivalent to 3 per cent of the company's gross revenue.
Third, as in previous years the bill provides authority for the government to make temporary advances to Canadian National Railways and Air Canada to meet deficiencies in operating revenues up to June 30, 1972. Such advances are repaid later in the year from the companies' revenues. If these prove inadequate, the insufficiency is covered by a parliamentary appropriation.
Fourth, the bill contains an option similar to that contained in the 1970 Financing and Guarantee Act which would enable Air Canada to borrow $114 million prior to July 1, 1972 either directly from Her Majesty or by means of a guaranteed public issue. It also would renew the authority for the Minister of Finance to guarantee debentures amounting to 13 million pounds to be issued in the period May 1, 1972 to December 31, 1976 by Air Canada in accordance with contractual obligations assumed by the airline prior to July 1, 1972.

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
Fifth, the bill contains a clause to increase to one billion dollars the limit on the amount of substituted securities that may be issued by the CNR in respect of any refunding pursuant to provisions of the CNR Refunding Act, 1955. The Financing and Guarantee Act of 1964 raised that ceiling to $680 million. The further increase of $320 million proposed in this bill would make adequate provision should a decision be taken to replace with longer term financing the temporary government loans authorized under section 7 of the 1955 refunding act.
Finally, the bill would provide for the appointment of the firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co. of the cities of Toronto and Montreal, chartered accountants, as auditors of Canadian National Railways for the calendar year 1972.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again this House is being asked to rubber stamp its approval of the expenditures of certain crown corporations during the past year. Once again we are being asked indirectly to approve the actions of these corporations during the past year, even though all members of the House know that we have little or no control over the policies of these corporations. In fact, about the only time that we hear from them is when they come to this House looking for money to pay their bills.
The fact that this annual exercise in futility has been going on for years does not make it any more valid. The fact that year after year members of the House deplore the custom of voting moneys which have already been spent does not make the custom any more palatable. Nor does it soothe the feelings of members on this side when they realize that, despite their annual objections and criticism, their suggestions for a review of the whole procedure-in fact, a review of the whole transportation policy-nothing changes from year to year. We are still being denied any effective voice in the conduct of Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. We are still told by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) that the National Transportation Act is the be-all and end-all, that the government is apparently quite satisfied with it. Not only parliament but the people of this country, who after all supply the money to pay the deficits of these two corporations, are effectively blocked by the provisions of an act which sets up quasi-judicial bodies which have put themselves beyond the law. Has anyone ever been known to launch a successful appeal with the Canadian Transport Commission?
But, Mr. Speaker, hope springs eternal and the members on this side continue year after year to debate the CN financing bill and to criticize it. In fact, sometimes it seems as if everyone wants to get into the act, to take a swipe at the CNR and to offer suggestions for improvements in service. Surely, this must be the reason that we go through this exercise year after year, for we cannot change anything. The money has been spent. Even if the opposition did refuse to allow the bill easy passage, I suppose the government would ram it through anyway, since this government is quite expert at ramming through unpalatable legislation.
I suppose this exercise will continue to be one of futility until this government is prepared to examine the rationale of its national transportation policy, to set priorities and
to determine what role our national carriers must play. This government must show leadership, must designate those services that are essential and must be provided, subsidized if necessary-this applies to all modes of transportation whether it be air, ground or water transpora-tion-and then insist that these carriers provide efficient services.
Until this government does that, about the only good that can come of this debate is the opportunity it gives us to examine the operations of the CNR and Air Canada, both here and in Committee, to criticize those operations and make suggestions. This is only right, for if these Crown corporations want this House to vote them money they should be prepared to submit their operations to a thorough and searching examination. This is the only time that this House has an opportunity to examine the activities of the CNR and Air Canada, and it is the only time that hon. members can make suggestions and recommendations on behalf of the people of Canada, who are not too happy about the manner in which these two corporations carry out their day to day operations.
Surely, the government owes the people of this country the duty not only to listen to their complaints but to take some action on them. This is where the government has failed the people of Canada shamefully. This is where a good share of the responsibility lies for failing to develop a national and rational transportation policy that is based not on profit alone but rather on the concept that transportation is essential to Canada, that where necessary services must be subsidized, whether they be in the form of highway, rail, air or water transport. The profit motive is important, but it should be secondary to the concept of providing essential public services.
This bill, as the parliamentary secretary has outlined, provides financing for Air Canada. In view of this I think it only proper that I say a few words about Air Canada, and in this regard I find myself in an awkward position. Since I have been subjected to the whims of Air Canada for the past four days, in my present mood I find it very difficult to be objective, but I should like to make some general remarks, leaving my colleagues to zero in on specifics, of which I know there are plenty.
I think the nature of one of the difficulties being faced was very well illustrated by Mr. Yves Pratte, chairman of the board and chief executive officer of Air Canada, when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications on June 22, 1971. Mr. Pratte was asked many questions about the airline's philosophy, about its rationale. Was the airline there to make money or to provide services? His reply was very interesting and I think gets right to the nub of the government's indecision on a transportation policy. Mr. Pratte said this:
The basic problem in so far as we at the management level are concerned is that we do not know what the mission of Air Canada is. We wish we knew. It is awfully difficult to manage any organization when one does not know what the purpose of the organization is: when you are told on the one hand that the purpose of the organization is to be as profitable as any private corporation and, on the other hand, that you are to provide service at all cost.
Is it any wonder that Mr. Pratte was confused as to what his duties are as chief executive officer of Air

March 6, 1972

Canada. He went on to say that he had offered ideas and made suggestions to the government, but came back to the point that the government had not laid down a clear-cut policy for him to follow. In other words, was it to be principally a profit making organization or was it to provide services where they were deemed essential? Mr. Pratte went on to say:
But this requires a definition of the role of the corporation which, I submit very respectfully, we do not have at the present time.
That was on June 22 last year. When reference was made to that statement in this House, I remember that the Minister of Transport expressed surprise that Mr. Pratte would say such a thing. However, he must have read the transcript of the evidence and realized that Mr. Pratte did indeed make that statement because in the Toronto Star of June 28, 1971 the minister is quoted as saying:
We would like to give Air Canada a clearcut mandate but it is hard to be precise. I have been working on this for two years.
The problem has existed longer than that, Mr. Speaker, but surely in two years this government could come up with some rational air policy. How much longer must we wait? When the minister and the management of Air Canada do now know what the mission of the corporation is, when there is not a transport policy worthy of the name for other means of transport either separately or in combination, it is unreasonable for this House to be asked to vote moneys to Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. The House and the public have a right to know how the taxpayers' money is being spent and the government has an obligation to define its policy objectives. The shareholders of a private corporation would laugh at directors who brought in such a request for money. The government has admitted publicly that it does not know where it is going or what its priorities are, yet it asks for another $600 million or more. I think this is completely ridiculous, but I shall let my colleagues zero in on some of the specific problems of Air Canada later.
Last week in this House, we heard speaker after speaker endorse the principle of equalization payments, a scheme designed to compensate the less affluent provinces for their unfavourable economic or geographical situation. At least one speaker pointed out the difficulties imposed upon the western and eastern extremities of this country by the high cost of transportation involved in competing in the markets of central Canada. They pointed out quite correctly that equalization of transportation costs was just as valid a proposition as transfer payments from the central government for social welfare, education and all the various purposes for which these transfer payments are used under the equalization principle.
It is an historic fact of confederation that the outlying parts of the country, both west and east, must have competitive transportation costs to and from the markets of central Canada. Not only were parts of the country cut off from their traditional markets in the United States by tariff barriers set up to protect central Canadian industry, and from those parts of the country which offer natural markets, but new problems were created, particularly in the Maritimes, by the fact that direct rail routes to the United States were replaced by a circuitous all-Canada rail line. In other words, essentially for purposes of defence, the rail line was taken by an all-Canada route
CNR and Air Canada
when the shortest route would have been through the United States. This has aggravated the problem of distance already suffered in these areas.
Is it any wonder that people in the Atlantic provinces are upset by the erosion of the Maritime protection established in the old Maritime Freight Rates Act? Under the old Railway Act, which was amended by the National Transportation Act, under the terms of subsection 326(5) no charges could be made unless authorized as follows:
"No tolls shall be charged by the company or by any person in respect of a railway or any traffic thereon until a by-law authorizing the preparation and issue of such tolls has been authorized by the Board"-
The reference is to the old Board of Transport Commissioners. This was one of the sections which was repealed, with the result that the railways or carriers do not have to get prior approval of rate increases. They simply announce a rate, allow the stated waiting period to pass and the tolls become effective on that date. It is all very well to say that there is provision for appeal to the CTC. In theory there is, but in practice no such thing exists because it is impossible for a private company to make an effective appeal. Each time a rate increase was announced, other members of the opposition and myself pleaded with the Minister of Transport to order the CNR to delay it until a new policy was devised, but he would not listen. He always said that he could not do it or, because of rising costs, the CNR must raise rates. I realize that costs are rising, but I am saying that we in the east and west have a constitutional right to have rising freight rate costs offset by direct transfer payments to the shipper or by some other means. All we ask is that the minister live up to his commitment that he would not allow reductions in subsidies or increases in freight rates unless and until some equivalent assistance was provided for the people affected.
But what has happened? We have been waiting for this government to act on some sort of national transportation policy. A recent issue of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission's monthly bulletin, Tips and Topics reports that:
For the eighth time in the past twenty-nine months, rail rates will increase on February 14, 1972.
That increase has come into effect.
The increase announced by the Railway Association of Canada on behalf of the Canadian railways, will range from 4 to 8 per cent.
The latest increase is another in what has become a pattern of an increase every six months since the lifting of the rail freight rate freeze on September 23, 1969. This succession of rail rate increases now stands at a cumulative total of 35 to 68 per cent (depending upon the rate level) for non-competitive rail rates and 19 to 40 per cent on competitive rail rates.
The minister said that, of course, there had been no increases for 10 years prior to that. That is true, but I want to point out to the House that the cumulative increase enacted following the lifting of the freeze has been more than would normally be expected in those 10 years. Those increases have exceeded the increases in any similar period since World War II, so that these freight rate increases cannot be justified by any trend in the rising cost of living or rising costs.
Why were these rates increased so rapidly? I think the answer is to be found in the fact that the railways no

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
longer have to seek prior approval of the federal regulatory body, nor do they have to justify these increases as was the case prior to 1967. Secondly, when the National Transportation Act was enacted in 1967, the railways were paid a transitional subsidy beginning in 1967 at $110 million and declining each year until its disappearance in 1974. This transitional subsidy was designed to compensate the railways in a broad way for uneconomic services which the railways were maintaining by the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission. I have no quarrel with elimination of the subsidy. I think any reasonable member of this House would realize that subsidies are not the best way to handle these problems.
But we in the Atlantic provinces are asking that the government follow the recommendation of the Atlantic premiers or of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission in 1969 when they agreed that it would be wise to phase out the subsidy but only-and here is the crux of the whole question which the government has conveniently overlooked-if the subsidies were replaced by an equivalent amount of money which should be allocated to shippers on some basis determined by an independent commission. We said, all right, phase out the subsidy but do not take it away unless it is replaced with something else. This, in itself, would be bad enough, but what we are now finding is that the phasing out of the subsidies has already started. They have been reduced by 25 per cent. Not only did the government not grant an equivalent amount of assistance to the shippers involved, but about a month later the railways raised their rates by an amount which would roughly offset the 25 per cent subsidy they lost. Here, we get it both ways.
Instead of having a new policy to replace the old one in order to give some assistance to our shippers, we now find the minister has embarked on a policy of taking away the assistance we had and at the same time allowing the railways to increase their rates. We do not know where it will end. It has reached the point where many of our major shippers are very concerned about the situation. I think I should read into the record at this time excerpts from a letter from the Secretary of the Maritime Co-operative Services Limited, which is one of the largest shippers in the maritime area. Mr. McEwen, the secretary, states:
We are further concerned that millions of dollars are being spent under DREE in the area to develop industry which has little hope of survival without a long-term transportation policy to move the products of these industries into the markets of central Canada or New England, U.S.A. The transportation factor seems to be largely ignored by the planners in the development of this industrialization.
I have heard my colleagues repeatedly take up this aspect with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). Certainly, the transportation factor is very much involved in manufacturing in the maritime area. Mr. McEwen continues by saying:
In our opinion, it would be better to use the money to add to the fund suggested by the premiers and equalize transportation on some point, such as Levis, Quebec and then industry could develop and operate competitively.
Here again, I have taken up this matter with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and have heard
my colleagues repeatedly refer to it. Millions of dollars are being pumped into the Atlantic area to create industries which have no reasonable chance of success, because once they start producing goods and wish to ship them out of the maritime area they find the transportation costs are so high they cannot compete in the markets of central Canada which are their natural markets.
The writer goes on to say:
We have watched, over the years, various secondary industries die.
He speaks about a small manufacturing company which produced wooden step ladders which gradually over the years, because of the rising freight rates, became less and less competitive until about five years ago it went out of business. He says:
We see the same thing happening to industries that have been developed recently with area incentive grants but no consideration being given to transportation.
So, this is what is happening in the Atlantic provinces. I believe the same situation exists in the other provinces which are faced with extremely high freight rates. This is why we continually call upon the government to get off its fanny and suggest some sort of a regional transportation policy. There are many other areas I could touch on because this whole field is very broad. It would be impossible for me to cover all of them, however, even if I had all day every day or if I had a week.
I should like to mention a matter about which many people probably do not think when they consider the exorbitant cost of transportation. Many people in this House who are shippers or businessmen probably know what the term "demurrage" means. Demurrage on railway cars is a charge levied which is supposed to be an incentive to unload cars quickly. The charge is, therefore, a penalty if cars are held beyond the free period, which is normally two days. This demurrage tariff is administered by the Canadian Car Demurrage Bureau, which is supposed to be an independent body, but is owned and controlled by the various railways in Canada. The substantial revenue derived from its operation is paid back to the railways. In spite of protestations otherwise by the railways, this organization has become a source of substantial revenues, and with the free hand it now has to levy whatever charges it wishes it is carrying its mandate to the fullest extent.
We always seem to come back to the Canadian Transport Commission. The CTC seems to be always at the root of all our troubles. Until the Canadian Transport Commission was set up, the Canadian Car Demurrage Bureau had to adopt the same procedure as the railways. It had to go to the Board of Transport Commissioners to have its tariff approved, but this is no longer necessary. The result is that since the change in the act, demurrage charges have been increased drastically to the point that they are now a major item of expense to any company using railway facilities. It is easy to get a car in, turn it around and get it out in many areas of central Canada but at the end of the line, as it were, these cars may be in an area on Friday where they are required to stay over the weekend because they cannot be hauled out. Up until recently, three free days were provided. If the last free day was a Friday, there would be no charge for the weekend. Now,

March 6, 1972

by an arbitrary ruling of the board, the shipper, if the car is not unloaded by Friday night, must pay the demurrage charges for Saturday, Sunday and Monday. One might say that this does not amount to much, but over a period of years it could involve thousands of dollars for shippers in the Maritimes and might mean the difference between a profit operation and a loss. Because of our distance from the central markets, the Atlantic provinces feel the effect of these charges to a much greater extent than other parts of the country.
Indeed, the transportation problems of the Atlantic provinces have always been serious. This fact was recognized at the time of confederation, but we received no protection in the terms of confederation similar to the Crow's Nest Pass rates which are applicable in western Canada. We receive no demurrage concessions such as those which are applicable at Thunder Bay. These demurrage charges are serious, but the most serious feature of this whole situation is that once again the CNR and Air Canada, and now the Canadian Demurrage Bureau are allowed to arbitrarily assess tariffs from which there is no effective appeal from them. The rapidly escalating costs of transportation are slowly strangling the development of the Atlantic region, and not only are we receiving no response to requests for change in government policy but the policies of the transportation agencies are making it impossible for the maritime manufacturer or feed producer to ship to or receive from the markets of central Canada.
Even though this is a routine financing bill such as we get every year, I still feel it is important because Parliament should tie down CNR and Air Canada until such time as the government comes up with a policy which will provide a service to Canadians in all parts of the country. Until the government is prepared to do that, we will not be prepared to grant them any further money. It is difficult to take such a stand in the House, but sometimes I think we should. At least we should refer this bill to the committee where, hopefully, we will receive some answers from the minister as to what he proposes to do and what the transportation policy for all parts of Canada is to be.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am entering the debate on this bill at this stage because my colleagues and I believe that this government, this parliament and the people of Canada, have permitted the railway and air services of this country to be contracted to the harm not only of individual Canadians but of communities of Canadians and that the time has come to call a halt to that process. We feel very strongly that the time has come to say to both the railway systems that the abandonment of rail lines, the closing down of local stations, and the dismissal of local agents must end, and that the real purpose of the transportation system must govern their actions instead of the totally false social approach which is now animating their policies.
The people of Canada granted tens of millions of dollars and tens of millions of acres of land to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and then when a number of railways failed, the people of this country paid and continue to pay hundreds of millions of dollars in debt to set up the
CNR and Air Canada
Canadian National Railways system. We built the first at the end of the nineteenth century with money and grants of land on which the CPR has built an immense financial, mineral and industrial empire, and we built the second, the Canadian National Railways, out of small railways that had failed. We did that almost immediately after the first world war.
I suggest to you, Sir, that the people of Canada spent these immense amounts of money and made these immense grants of land not for the purpose of these organizations developing some profit. They built these railways, spent this money and gave grants of land because a country the size of Canada cannot live unless there is an adequate railways system from one end of the country to the other. The people of Canada spent these moneys and gave these grants because they recognized that it is otherwise impossible to support an agricultural industry dependent on exports in large measure and on movement across the country as far as feed grains and related products are concerned. They gave these moneys and these grants of land because they recognized that all the sections of Canada's economy required a transportation system. They did that in the days when the air transportation system was not yet available. These moneys were not spent for the CPR to make profits; they make enough profits even though they may not make them on passenger railway service. The money was not given to the CNR to make profits when we took over the bankrupt railways. They were built for the purpose of serving the people of Canada. Both railways have failed in their duty and should stand condemned as failing many communities, particularly in the west. Both railways stand condemned as having failed the economic needs of regions of Canada distant from the centre by their inconsiderate and continual increase in freight rates without a sufficient change in rates to fit the situation of the Atlantic provinces or of western Canada.
This is one of the two or three points I want to make, and I make it as emphatically as I can. This is the opportunity for me to say that the Canadian Pacific Railway is an organization without conscience. Having built its strength and its power on moneys and on land given it by the people of Canada, it is now a railway, an air, a bus and a steamship organization. It has transportation systems in the air, on the water and on rail as well as on highways. It is an organization that has immense oil, gas and mineral reserves and subsidiaries right across the country. It owns large tracts of real estate and makes very large profits on the whole. The entire CPR empire makes very large annual profits, and yet they do not have the sense of obligation to Canada which established that organization, which paid for its building, and which made it possible for it to grow. They do not have that sense of obligation to Canada which would require them to continue the passenger service because it may not be or probably is not profitable.
I say the same thing to the CNR leadership, Mr. Speaker. The difference between the publicly owned corporation and the privately owned corporation is that, contrary to what the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) thought, the CNR officers can be brought before a corn-
550

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
mittee of parliament, and undoubtedly will be there to be questioned, but not the CPR officers. I say to the CN: your company is no longer accepting its responsibility to carry out its duty as a transportation service.
For a number of years, working with some of the railway unions from about 1952 to about 1962,1 had occasion to take a deeper interest in railway services across this country. I tried to learn a little about the railway services, and particularly about passenger service. What I learned was that there is no railway in the world that makes money out of its passenger service, not even those that run on the eastern seaboard of the United States where the population is great, where communities are close to each other, and where trains do not have to run across an entire continent, say from Vancouver to Halifax, Winnipeg to Toronto, or whatever it may be.
In the eastern U.S. seaboard, the railways lost money on passenger service on the whole. True, there were seasons when they made money, seasons when passenger service was profitable, but many other seasons when it was unprofitable. There just is not any railway that can make profits out of passenger service. I have not yet read an expert on railway economy who recognizes that passenger service can be profitable at all times. But any government or any country that has any sense of priorities and of purpose obliges its railways to give passenger service. That is one of the reasons for the existence of railways. This is true regardless of the fact that the provision of passenger service may be undertaken at a loss, as undoubtedly it is in Canada. I do not think the railways in Canada are making money out of passenger service, or ever did make money out of it. But they were established for the purpose of giving service to communities.
On this point I merely want to add that the reason my colleagues and I feel so strongly that the two railway systems have betrayed their obligations is not solely that there are individuals in some northern parts of Ontario, or in some small communities in Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta who cannot now have this necessary transportation service. This is extremely important, but it is not the only reason. In addition to the fact that people are being inconvenienced, communities are being destroyed. It is not only that individuals are being inconvenienced in not having the railway service to which they are entitled, it is the fact that when you close a railway station or an agency, and this is followed up by the closing of the elevator at a remote locality in the prairie provinces, then a whole host of other activities follow, and communities are on the verge of dying. This is where the thoughtless acts of the railway companies become most apparent.
So far as the New Democratic Party is concerned right across this country, we say that enough is enough. From now on, passenger service ought to be provided for Canadians, and local stations and agencies ought to be continued. That is the purpose of a railway.
I was a member of this House, Mr. Speaker, when the Transport Act was passed setting up the Canadian Transport Commission. I remember the then minister of transport, Mr. Pickersgill, piloting the bill through the House.

speechtext:
He piloted the bill through the House of Commons, and then piloted the minister of transport into the position of president of the Canadian Transport Commission. I have had the pleasure of knowing Mr. Pickersgill for many years but I say, Sir, that in carrying out the policies and the duties of that commission, the various parts of it are showing a reactionary unconcern for the needs of the people of Canada, are showing a reactionary concentration on the dollars and cents involved.
In my opinion, the Canadian Transport Commission is much more an agency of the railways than it is of this parliament or of the people of Canada, and that this cannot any longer be tolerated. If the railways need an agency they can pay for it themselves. We should not have to pay for it. If Mr. Pickersgill and his associates want to act for the Canadian Railway Association they are free to do so, but not at public expense. The public is paying the members of the Canadian Transport Commission in order to make certain that the public interest is served by the organizations answerable to the commission. However, that is not what the commission has been doing, whether with respect to the railway companies, the air companies, or indeed Bell Telephone, an organization that has been rooking the Canadian consumer for God knows how many years. Almost every time Bell comes before the CTC with an application for an increase, after a long falderol and inquiry, by some inconceivable coincidence it is able to get the increase. I should not say this happens always. There have been delays and changes, but eventually Bell is able to prove its case, no matter how indefensible its case may be.
I take the occasion of this bill to voice on behalf of our party our strongest protest against the philosophy and thrust of the CTC as related to the abandonment of railway services, as related to rates set by the railways, and as related to all the other agencies and bodies that come under its jurisdiction. It is my firm conviction, after watching it functioning since it came into existence, that it is not carrying out its function as a safeguarder of the public interest, but in effect is an agent of the transportation companies rather than of this parliament and of the people of Canada. That is true no matter in what direction you look.
The hon. member for Moncton was entirely right when he said that one of the main causes of inequality of opportunity, of economic circumstances, and of the level and standard of services in those parts of Canada distant from the centre, like the Atlantic provinces, like the west, and like Northern Ontario, has been the cost of transportation.
One of the legitimate, sensible, rational and just ways of assisting the disadvantaged areas of Canada-I do not say it is the only way because more needs to be done-is to set up the necessary differentials, the necessary subsidies if the case requires them, to rid these areas, particularly the Atlantic provinces, of the immense disadvantage they have in the fact of transportation distances, and in the fact of the costs of transportation. This is something that has been recognized in Canada over many years but has never become part of an integrated transportation system.
The third point I want to touch on briefly, and I do not intend to speak very long today, is to protest against the continuing and determined effort of the CTC, and obvi-

March 6, 1972

ously the policies of the government, to increase the number of private air carriers and to give them more and more of the feeder lines, more and more of the air transportation routes in Canada. At the moment when our publicly owned air transport company gets out of the red and begins to generate its own surpluses which it will need to assist in the expansion and renewal of equipment made necessary by modern developments and provide that service which, if left alone, it would continue to provide, big and little private corporations, led by CP Air, enter the field and the Canadian Transport Commission gives to these small or large transport organizations rights and privileges which, before then, had belonged to Air Canada. This means that in many parts of Canada, and most of northern Ontario is one of them, the people will not be served by Air Canada at all. They will be served either by CP Air or, more likely, by one of these other, small transport companies.
I do not object to the thrust, courage or enterprise of an individual or group of individuals wishing to set up some air company. I am not saying that such people should not be allowed to develop their business. What I am saying is that, in the long run, it is shortsighted and stupid to allow them to do so at the expense of the potential income and development of Air Canada. I am saying that CP Air particularly ought not to be given that kind of advantage. Air Canada, it seems to me from my study of it, and I might easily be wrong, may welcome this opportunity for lessened service. The company may even have desired it, because in the process it would lose some of its headaches as well.
I am never in favour of bureaucrats, whether in the public service, in Crown corporations or with private companies, who want to take the line of least resistance and fewest headaches. As I say, Air Canada may have wanted this. Yet I venture to suggest that in 10, 15 or 20 years a great many people will be sorry for what has happened as the opportunities for Air Canada grow fewer and as the demands for capital increase greatly. Then Air Canada, instead of having generated some of its own investment and replacement capital, will have to come to an increasing extent to parliament and ask for loans, grants, underwritings or what have you.
I do not think that makes sense. We had sense enough to set up a publicly owned air corporation. We ought not to interfere with the possibility of its future growth by handing out licenses without first considering what the consequences of these actions will be in future and how they will affect the people of Canada. And, instead of standing up and making these demands from the CTC, Air Canada has been acquiescing in developments which are bound to be fundamentally hurtful to it in the long run, if not in the short run. The company has cut down service constantly across this country and that, too, I regret very much.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a brief word about the capitalization of the CPR. I heard, during my recent few days of visiting to the western part of this country, that the CNR is losing money. Like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), Mr. Speaker, I made some non-partisan, non-election visits to western cities not long ago.

speechtext:
All the time in the lobbies here, and particularly in the lobby with my friends from the Tory party who, I notice, were robbed this morning of their major election issue with the recapture of Geoffroy in Spain, one hears the refrain, as one does elsewhere across Canada, that the CNR is losing money, that here we have an example of a publicly owned corporation and it loses money. Actually, Mr. Speaker, when the CNR capital setup was changed some years ago, and I was glad then that it was changed, the change did not go far enough. The CNR continues to carry a debt which it ought not to continue carrying. It is stupid to continue loading it with that debt. The CNR capital structure ought to be changed again, to the point where the CNR does not carry the debt which was originally undertaken when we nationalized the little bankrupt railways that make up the CNR.
Some years ago I asked someone to calculate how much a person or estate, or what have you, would make if $100 were invested in one of the companies that went bankrupt in 1918, 1919 and 1920. We assumed that the original share would be changed into a share of the CNR. I forget exactly what the term for such securities is, and I forget how the matter was handled. I wanted to know what the return would be for a person or estate on an investment of $100. You will be surprised to learn that the present return would be about three or four times the amount that was invested only 40 or 50 years ago, Mr. Speaker. I ask, how much longer are you to go on making the public treasury pay for a publicly owned utility on that kind of base. Therefore, I say that the capitalization of the CNR ought to be changed so that the railway ceases to carry the immensely heavy burden of debt and interest payments that that involves.
I want to conclude by saying something that some of my colleagues have said better than I can claim to say it. The point I want to emphasize in our discussion of this bill is that the people of Canada urgently require an integrated transportation policy. I, personally, believe that a utility like transportation ought to be all publicly owned. Canada is only one of two countries in the western world in which a privately owned railway system operates. The other country is the United States. No matter whether you look at Britain, France, West Germany, Denmark, Norway, Spain, Australia, New Zealand or Japan, you will find that the railway system is publicly owned. Railway service and transportation services in general are a public service. They are a public utility and not areas out of which private profit ought to be made. They are necessary services. A transportation system is necessary not only for the pleasure of people who use it; it is primarily necessary for the movement of goods, services and people. It is necessary for the good of the country as a whole and for the building of the economy of the country. This is true particularly for a country like Canada which depends so greatly on the export market in so many economic areas. Therefore I make no apology for having said to the presi-

dent of the CPR when I was a very young man that, if I had the opportunity, I would nationalize his railway. That was said-and I know I should not admit this-in January, 40 years ago. I do not doubt that the CPR will be nationalized eventually, either by my party in power or, to judge from what has happened in past years in many areas, by some other party in power. They will finally recognize the need for it.
In any event, we require an integrated transportation policy that takes into account all four major means of transport; air, road, rail and water. It must integrate these four major means of transport in some meaningful way for all parts of this country, and place all modes of transport under one really effective control, in the hands of government and Parliament through an agency. In this way it will serve the public interest and not be the lobby for the transportation companies that the CTC now is in many respects. In order to have an integrated transportation policy, we must have the courage to take over a large part of the CPR, if not all, in order to take over the profitable as well as the unprofitable, so that we will have public control.
The CPR now has a rail company, airline, more than one bus company, steamships, hotels, trucking services, minerals, oil and gas. Every time officers of the CPR appeared before boards on which I represented labour unions and shed some tears about its awful financial condition, I thought to myself I had not heard a more amusing comedy before and never expected to hear it again. The crocodile tears which the management of the CPR is constantly dropping are just outrageous. It has been a very successful empire. We ought to take over this company and place it under public ownership and control, not for any doctrinaire reason, but in order to integrate our transportation system in all four areas. That is and has been my own personal view for many years. Only in this way can we have a transportation system that will serve the people of Canada well, both now and in the future.
If I remember the order, this bill is scheduled to be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I am sure the members of that committee will be wise and determined enough to call the officers of the CNR and Air Canada to appear before that committee this year, as has been the case in the past. I can assure the House that our members of the committee will demand much better explanations than we have had in the past with regard to the unacceptable reduction in passenger service and the closing of offices and agencies which have taken place throughout Canada, particularly in the prairie provinces. Although I have not looked into the situation, I hope it will also be possible to call spokesmen for the CTC before that committee. I hope the members of the committee from all parties will unitedly tell Mr. Pickersgill and his associates that Canada will no longer accept the reduction in passenger and other services which the railways have undertaken to the detriment of the building of communities, particularly in western Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the debate in the House, Bill C-4 will be referred to the Transport and Communications Committee for detailed study. Earlier today, I listened to the comments of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) on the Canadian Pacific, which is a private corporation and Canadian National and Air Canada, which are government corporations.
He admitted that private enterprise makes huge profits on providing the same services as Canadian National while the latter company is calling on us for $210,800,000 to cover its deficit and Air Canada is asking for $114 million. This makes a total of $333 million, a third of a billion dollars, to support public enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, I should readily recognize that railways, Air Canada and other carriers are public services, to be encouraged, supported and improved in order that they may provide services to the whole population of Canada. However, when it comes to saying that we should nationalize private enterprise to improve services, I am not at all in agreement with the hon. member for York South.
According to his theories, to improve the administration of justice and law we should nationalize lawyers, turn them into civil servants, ciphers such as the employees of Canadian National or those of our transportation systems.
Private enterprise proves that it can operate and provide better services at a profit over a given period whereas a public enterprise must provide better service, even without profit. That is public enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, I should advise the Canadian Transport Commission to hire the hon. member for York South and appoint him president of Canadian National at the earliest. It pays better, since he would be getting $100,000 to $125,000 a year. He would be in the right place. Moreover, being so persuasive and so determined and so well informed about nationalization, state control and socialization, he could no doubt, as president of the Canadian National, improve on our present services.
I made a trip to western Canada last year. I went by the Canadian Pacific and came back by the Canadian National. The difference between the two is as great as that between night and day.
On the CP, the service is faultless: good food, good service all the way as far as Victoria or Vancouver.
I came back by the CN, through Edmonton and Saskatoon, through the north. It was completely different. The coaches were dirty; it was easy to see that those responsible were not there; the employees were like people working from 9 to 5; their work was only a job to them. The CN does not have to make profits; we need only vote them some $219 million at the end of the year to make up its deficits.
With all this, we find, as the hon. member was saying a moment ago, that some rail services are abandoned. In my area, the CN has abandoned its Rouyn-Noranda-Tas-chereau service; the run between Montreal and Quebec, to come back toward Cochrane through the Abitibi region, and Temiscamingue, brings in a profit because of the forestry operations of Domtar at Lebel-sur-Quevillon and the forestry operations in the Lasarre area. The service

was improved at the rate of approximately ten miles per year.
In any event, I have known the railway service in that area for at least 35 or 40 years and, instead of 22 hours to go from Montreal to Amos, as was the case in the past, one now needs 18 or 19 hours. That is quite an improvement! The railway track is just about impossible and we do get thrown about; a person lying in bed is sure to remain wide awake, such is the lack of comfort-

My colleague from Champlain (Mr. Matte) has taken this train to Abitibi and found that this was the case as far as Parent.
So, tracks are poorly maintained!
At the end of the year, the Directors of the Canadian National-the Administration office-hastened to submit their estimates to us, saying: "We need $125,265,000 for new railway property. This is for new branch lines." Some are being built to connect Rouyn to Taschereau, but others are required for an amount of $19,000,000.
For equipment $44 million are needed; for telecommunications $22,437,000; for hotels $3,026,000.
CNR hotels lose money whereas CP hotels prosper.
Since the private sector prospers, we must nationalize it at once so that it may lose money. That is socialism! That is what elimination of free initiative brings about. If you deprive someone of initiative, you kill him; he is no longer interested in business. On the contrary, if you give him the opportunity to make the most of his talents, to be creative rather than crush him, you allow him to improve the living conditions in a country such as ours. We can see it throughout the world.
The hon. member for York South told us: There is no country in the world where the communication system is not state-owned. I took a train from Moscow to Leningrad in 1965, a state-owned train; it was worse that the old train in Abitibi. Why? Because personal initiative has disappeared; it has been suppressed. No one can set up a railway company today in the USSR, in Czechoslovakia or in any other socialist country in the world. Everything is state-owned. Even the taxi transportation system is state-owned. The cab drivers are civil servants. Everyone is a government employee. The government decides in the place of the individual. This is contrary to common sense!
We should not nationalize the Canadian Pacific; instead, we should sell the Canadian National to the Canadian Pacific because the latter operates at a profit. To make up the difference, the government should, while doing its duty, ensure that the means of transport serve the public
adequately, not through state gimmicks but by setting up agencies made up of responsible human beings and not "numbers".
Mr. Speaker, I was speaking of the lines the Canadian National had abandoned. A while ago, someone told me that the same company has a reserve fund for its
CNR and Air Canada
employees; $650 million were taken out of that fund and loaned at 4 per cent to other agencies, there being, it seems, too much money in the fund. However, they forget to raise the pensions of retired employees.
The Canadian National has problems, like every body else. Workers are dismissed after 30 or 40 years of service. They are no longer useful, right. However, the pension system should provide those people with an income equivalent to their former wages, since they have already paid contributions for their years of service. Instead of tampering with their pension fund it should be used for the benefit of those who spent their lives in the service of the Canadian National or other railroad companies.
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I feel that Bill C-4 is only a repetition of former bills. Indeed, the Canadian National or Air Canada never show a profit but deficits always while the Canadian Pacific always shows a profit, even with its airlines.
When CP Air was servicing my region why has it been replaced by Air Canada? Air Canada says that this service is not economical and someday it will give it up to Nordair. But why was this run taken away from CP Air if Air CAnada finds it uneconomical? There are three flights a day and the planes seem to be full each time. It is therefore an economical operation and this is why we asked them to improve the service. We are prepared to supply them the funds required provided we have the services in return.
The same thing applies to the CN. We are now voting $219 million in grants to our national railways and this company decides at a given moment to wage unfair competition against the private trucking industry by adopting exceedingly low rates precisely because it is subsidized by the government. We should grant similar amounts to the private sector if we want to have fair competition. But we should not tax the truckers to meet the deficit of a competing CN.
This is unfair and we should be able to establish criteria under which the private sector will not have to pay taxes to offset CN deficits.
To tax the Brazeau Transport Company or the Compa-gnie de camionnage du Quebec to pay CN deficits while it is engaged in the same kind of transportation-even though the member for York South finds nationalization quite fair and even commendable-I maintain this is pure and simple confiscation of private enterprise and an obstacle to normal operations of Canadian transport companies.
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues will be following carefully in committee the clause by clause study of this bill so as to determine what is wrong with the operations and with the administration of our national railways and Air Canada. We are not asking for the eliminations of those services. On the contrary, we are prepared to grant the required credits provided however they are supplied. If the credits passed by Parliament are used only to pay senior civil servants or strikers we are not at all interested. These expenses will not be paid by union leaders but by Canadian tax payers.
