Then, when we are asked to make up a $219 million deficit, we should understand that it is the result of all the strikes which cost a lot to Canada. Canadian taxpayers pay for that. The hon. member for York South may like it but I do not. That is why we say to union officials: Instead of distributing boxing gloves to Canadian workers, why not try to be peacemakers, so as to enable employees to get along with the employers? Instead of stirring up hatred among classes, why not foster comprehension between workers and employer's, who also have problems. Maybe they are not "9 to 5" people, as we call them, but they are up at 7 in the morning, still working at midnight and not paid for overtime. We do not think of that.
People like the hon. member for York South protest against exploiters, against private enterprise. Most private enterprise owners in Canada get a smaller net income than the hon. member for York South. It is easy to be a socialist at $100,000 or $50,000 a year. But when the owner of a small grocery store who works very hard to earn $15,000 or $20,000 a year is being told: My boy, the minimum hourly wage of your employees is $2, or else you will be fined, he is in danger of going bankrupt because we look upon him as an exploiter. It is easy for people with annua] salaries of $50,000 or $100,000 to tell people getting $20,000: You are an exploiter, you destroy small wage earners.
Mr. Speaker, there should be a limit to riduculing people and belittling their personal initiative, then trying to control everything through government action. Canadians do not want the government to poke its nose into all their personal affairs. The less nosing on the part of the government, the better it will be unless one is a socialist as in that case people probably lose courage. They say to the government: Make the decisions for me. Take my salary! Spend it the way you like and let me know what is left for me at the end.
As I have already said: let us continue to live in the present system. We will be heading towards socialism. Twenty years ago, I said: "Within 10 or 20 years, when you receive your pay cheques, the cheque stub will be at least twice as long as the cheque itself". This is what is happening today. The cheque Stub is at least twice as long as the cheque itself which means that so much money is deducted for unemployment insurance, so much for provincial and federal taxes, medical insurance, old age pension, union dues and super annuation, to the extent that the cheque stub is very long.
Within the next ten years, we will only receive the stub to acquaint us with the way the government has spent our pay cheque. We will then have complete socialism and the government will decide for us.
This is exactly what is happening, Mr. Speaker, because we are witnessing the establishment of programs such as this one, a nationalization program, a government system under which we are asked to pay for deficits year after year.
I agree that we pay for deficits in order to obtain services, but I notice that services are being reduced while deficits keep increasing. This is what I find unnatural. Let us increase services, let us improve them and pay for them. I quite agree, for this is absolutely natural-but let us not pretend as we are doing at present.
[Mr. Caouette.J
Mr. Speaker, in this bill we are asked to vote $333 million for the operation of our transportation system which is related to the government and is a nationalized enterprise.
As far as private enterprise is concerned, we do not hear of the Canadian Pacific Railways asking for any money to make up its deficits. No, that company makes profits. As I was saying at the beginning, rather than abolishing the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is a profitable operation, let us sell the Canadian National to the Canadian Pacific Railways; this way, it could be that next year we will have saved $219 million on what we are spending this year, and that this company will help the Canadian National to make profits.
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and myself advocate solutions designed to remedy this situation. We are quite aware that we have to pay for services. We do not object to this, but let us improve services to the same extent that we have to pay for deficits. Covering the deficits will then allow for the development of real services for the greater well-being of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to join in this debate, which is more a discussion of our transportation problems and ills, a subject that will be explored very thoroughly by the committee. This debate is particularly well timed, since just a few days ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) and the appropriate provincial authorities announced the final decision on the location of a new airport facility for the central Ontario region, particularly the Toronto-centred region, as well as an improvement in the air terminal facilities in southern Ontario.
My riding is specifically affected because part of the new airport proper is to be in my constituency; indeed, a lot of the flight patterns will be over a great part of my constituency. In view of this I am now beginning to come to grips in a very real way with the problems that a major airport causes the residents of a delightful part of Ontario that is close to metropolitan Toronto. Some rather serious problems will have to be faced by some. Although I am sure these will be resolved to the extent that that is possible, it does not detract from the fact that wherever an airport is sited there is some disruption caused local residents.
In this particular case I think all agree, in fairness, that a wiser selection could not have been made, and I think the co-operation between the federal government and the provincial government was the key to making certain that a wise decision was made. I say that with a little bit of sadness because I, myself, am not happy, quite frankly, that the new airport is to be located in part of my riding. But the people of York North are sensible people, particularly at election time, and they realize that such a decision would affect some people no matter where the airport had been located. They are not happy that they are the people affected, but they are counting on me and many others to make certain that its major effects are mitigated.
March 6, 1972

This is a time for us to think of what we must face in terms of transportation. We cannot think of transportation in terms of airports alone but rather as a total concept, in terms of the social and economic impact that a major transportation facility has on the country.
Shortly after I entered this House in November 1968, I made a speech on somewhat the same subject as this, and I note that the other day the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales) also had something to say on the matter. I have been doing some work on a more comprehensive transportation plan because I feel we should be thinking in terms of where we go from here. We have an air plan that should satisfy our needs for the next 20 years or so, but we must look far beyond that. To think that the present concept is the answer to our transportation problem is not good enough.
I should like to suggest a logical projection of our transportation requirements over the next two or three decades beyond the time when this new facility will be well in use and perhaps overloaded. I take into consideration the natural industrial development areas and the need to remove the growth pressures from our major cities. Included in this proposal, and the key to it, is the accelerating growth of air transport for both goods and people. The result of my studies would be a major air terminal approximately midway between Toronto and Montreal, serviced by high speed surface transport joining these two cities and the air terminal. Such a transportation corridor would spawn planned residential and industrial communities along its route. The consequence should be a growing interdependence between French and English speaking Canada. Its immediate effect should be to capture the imagination of Canadians and focus their thinking toward the next 20 to 30 years which would be required to complete the first stages of this plan which I propose to outline. Even this time frame would require the earliest possible commitment to the concept, not to the program but to the concept.
Ste Scholastique and the new Toronto region airport should satisfy our air transport terminal requirements for close to a generation. Projections for the future indicate a sharp increase in air travel surpassing any growth we have seen since World War II. A substantially greater growth curve is indicated for air cargo. While these projections are difficult to make, and I am trying to get some more enlightened projections, I think they are important indeed. In spite of larger aircraft, the volume of traffic itself will present problems of air and noise pollution, safety and physical handling of both people and goods which will dwarf present considerations. One answer is to provide a major facility roughly equidistant between Toronto and Montreal which will alleviate the congestion and environmental problems which plague areas within a wide radius of any major airport.
The Kingston area appears to have many advantages. It is roughly equidistant and it already possesses the basic infrastructure of a major community. To the south is Lake Ontario and to the north vast areas with relatively sparse population. The environmental consequences of increased air traffic will be minimal relative to other areas. It is possible that the existing air base at Trenton
CNR and Air Canada
has many of the same advantages and a great advantage is that it exists, if not equidistant. It could conceivably be an alternative site.
While it is difficult to project technological development in the aero-space field, it may be assumed that air vehicles will increase in size, and long range flights of transcontinental and transocean traffic will increase at the greatest rate. Indeed, it is an integral part of this concept to reduce a major segment of the short haul air traffic. The balance of short haul traffic could continue to be handled at existing airports already adjacent to the major urban areas. The key to an airport facility remote from the major cities is high speed ground transportation enabling passengers to reach the airport or their ultimate destination in the minimum possible time. For practical purposes, this should be under one hour: distance itself is not the factor, but time is.
The suggested location is in the 150 to 175 mile range for both Toronto and Montreal. It therefore follows that average ground speeds in excess of 200 miles per hour will be necessary for the ground transport. Existing technology to achieve these speeds in comfort already exists. Prototype development is under way in France, Germany and Japan, while promising research is being undertaken in the U.S. and even Canada, if one wishes to include the CN-United Aircraft Turbotrain. The Germans, particularly, have some new technology which is interesting according to my studies.
It can reasonably be assumed that satisfactory resolution of the technical difficulties involved in this development will be accomplished before this proposal is at the implementation stage. The technology is there now and prototypes are under way. It is certainly within our capacity. It is likely that the commitment to this project will accelerate development, and it is possible that Canada could concentrate a significant portion of its research and development activity in this very field.
In a country as large and as sparsely settled as is Canada, transportation is as vital to its growth as it was when our present railways were conceived. Indeed, it is the same type of vision and commitment which is called for at this time. I am just reading Pierre Berton's book on the building of the CPR, and it is interesting to see an example of this type of vision. I hope we do not experience the politics or the business practices engaged in at that time, but there certainly was a great deal of vision. However, it was not a Liberal government in office at that time, so I am sure things would be better today.
Our existing rail beds would provide the essential right-of-way. It would be necessary to improve these substantially, but as new high speed ground transport is unlikely to utilize conventional trackage, this would be an integral part of the development. The important consideration is that the right-of-way exists, though some deviation might prove necessary, and the use of elevated or underground systems in whole, or in part, cannot be rejected. It is possible that the system could involve all three levels, that is, ground, underground and elevated. Propulsion could range from diesel to nuclear, jet to vacuum, and possibly gravitational, but this I leave to the scientists.
With the ability to reach a midway point between Montreal and Toronto in less than one hour, it will be possible

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
to continue via surface transport between these cities in approximately two hours, or slightly more when intermediate stops are taken into consideration. When transport to and from airports is considered, it presently takes in excess of this time to complete an inter-city trip by air.
With high speed surface transport terminating in central areas of the cities and tying into existing and projected subway facilities, it is reasonable to assume that travellers would use the ground facility for the entire journey and at considerable benefit in time, comfort and convenience. I cannot give the precise percentages at this time, but a significant percentage of the take-offs and landings in both Toronto and Montreal are for flights between these points. By putting these travellers back on the ground, a considerable amount of air traffic would be eliminated. With the relief of this pressure on our airports, the growth of other short-haul traffic, that is, New York, Chicago, Winnipeg, Quebec, Halifax, Ottawa, Boston, Windsor, London, etc. could well be accommodated with existing facilities such as Dorval, Ste Scholastique, Malton and the new Toronto region airport.
Curfew regulations applicable at airports adjacent to cities are a major social and economic consideration. These may be substantially relaxed or eliminated at a more remote location. It is likely that noise levels will be significantly reduced or noise eliminated by the time a concept such as this reaches fruition. With or without the noise consideration, air congestion and ground facilities would be under-utilized during the hours from midnight to seven or eight a.m. The elimination of curfews would enable 24 hour operation with cargo aircraft being accommodated during the low passenger traffic hours.
It must be assumed that the airport would not be located immediately adjacent to the city of Kingston itself, but could be as close as ten to 25 miles, the latter figure being preferable. Major residential development within a radius of perhaps up to 25 miles of the airport would be curtailed.
A further development would be the use of cargo containers which could be accommodated by regular aircraft and the high speed surface vehicles. This has been done successfully for water/rail transport and could be readily adapted to air/rail. It is another area for Canadian research and development.
I see it is five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: POLLUTION

speakeroldname: Mr. Lincoln M. Alexander (Hamilton West) moved:
subtopic: POLLUTION
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RESEARCH ON WASTE DISPOSAL METHODS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should initiate a national research and development program in respect of methods of proper and economic solid-waste disposal, including studies directed to the conservation of natural resources by reducing the amount of waste and unsalvageable materials and by recovery and utilization of potential resources in solid wastes; and provide technical and financial assistance to provincial and municipal governments and multi-governmental agencies in the planning, development, and conduct of solid-waste disposal programs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity of once again bringing to the attention of hon. members a problem which I have pointed out on two prior occasions on a private member's notice of motion. I am pleased to see the interest that is usually exhibited when I bring it back, and I know that government members will of course have some constructive criticism to offer of this motion. They may also raise some points which have made it necessary to move in this area to a greater extent than has been the case in the past.
My motion perhaps could be broken down into three parts. I say there should be initiated a national research and development program in respect of methods of proper and economic solid waste disposal. I see nothing wrong with the suggestion made, because obviously we are all in favour of pollution control. It is pollution control I am talking about, while at the same time having the opportunity to reclaim waste and turn it into a profit. I believe this is the sort of thing we are interested in because obviously, as has been stated, the United States spends billions of dollars to bury waste materials while at the same time millions of dollars could be reclaimed if only we had a co-ordinated effort to ascertain what type of material could be reclaimed, whether it is economically feasible to do so, and whether in fact there is a market for it. Notwithstanding how small the market may be, I would still impress upon the government the fact that this is an area in which we should not be concerned about an overall profit but rather whether, in fact, it is feasible to become involved in the reclamation of waste whereby we, in turn, attempt to reduce the ever-growing pollution.
Secondly, I should like someone to indicate whether, in fact, studies are to be undertaken. I know now that, as a result of governments having had the opportunity to do much of the research in certain areas, it is time that the type of research of which I am speaking now should be undertaken by the private sector. In this way we would be able to make some use, and good use, of the special talents required for a problem which faces us now and, perhaps
March 6, 1972

at the same time, relieve the unemployment situation as it relates to those of higher learning at this particular time. When I receive letters from persons who possess Ph.D's who tell me they cannot acquire work, then I believe there is something wrong with our system. They should at least be given an opportunity to further their education by attempting to bring about solutions to problems which at this particular time have been practically untouched by the federal level of government. I say this with a great deal of respect because I feel that, in order to pacify those who believe we are not involved with this matter, the federal government must step in, even though someone will tell me it is a provincial matter, in order to give us some idea whether or not this is a matter of high priority.
The last time this subject was brought to our attention, I asked some questions which were placed on the order paper. I asked which department, if any, bears primary responsibility for the development of research or demonstration projects to deal with solid waste disposal. Then, as a second question, I asked on what dates and by whom were recommendations made to the Department of National Health and Welfare advocating research studies into the problem of solid-waste disposal as indicated by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance on December 14, 1970 in Hansard at page 2026-2027. As I understand the answer, it is anticipated that the new Department of the Environment will bear primary responsibility for the development of research or demonstration projects to deal with solid-waste disposal. This reply was tabled through the courtesy of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) on January 25, 1971. I should like to know, in fact, what the department is doing in terms of the suggestions I have placed before it. In Hamilton we have tried to make strides in this area by having a form of pulverizer which, as I understand it, has been a welcome addition to the waste disposal facilities.
Let me point out that in 1960, as reported in the Hamilton Spectator sometime in 1971, Hamilton threw away about 185,000 tons of garbage. In 1971 there were some 285,000 tons. This is an increase from 625 pounds per person in the 1960's to 700 pounds per person at the present stage. I think what I am concerned about is the lack of appreciation of the problems being faced by municipalities, because obviously they do not have the money to make the capital expenditure required for the type of project necessary to ascertain just which type of solid-waste disposal method is acceptable, feasible or economical. It is in this area that my motion indicates we should be providing technical and financial assistance to provincial governments, municipal governments and multi-governmental agencies in the planning and development of solid-waste disposal programs.
Lately, the province of Ontario has commissioned people of some expertise on this subject. They brought out a report in February of 1971. The authors of this report were Professors Clark and Brown, the former a chemical engineer and the latter a mineral engineer, both of whom are pursuing their professions at Queen's University in Canada. I was very impressed by the conclusion reached in the report regarding the recommendations. One of their recommendations should perhaps solidify our thinking in terms of the importance of the need for
Pollution
action. The report is entitled Municipal Waste Disposal, Problem or Opportunity. It reads in part:
The current problem of solid waste disposal should be regarded as an opportunity for Canadian originality and foresight to develop the means for conserving natural resources, preserving the environment and demonstrating that organizations, communities and individuals can effectively co-operate in a common cause.
I find that the conclusions reached in this very candid and very important expose are very disturbing because it was just published in February 1971. With your patience, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote at some length from the report. It reads:
It is found that Canada has lagged the United States both in terms of legislation and the investigation of the disposal and treatment of municipal wastes. Data on the nature and quantity of municipal wastes is not available and no methods other than the traditional means of burial or incineration have been employed in Canada. Furthermore there is no organization in Canada which currently serves as an authoritative source of knowledge; neither is there a centre of research and development in this field. The newly created Waste Management Branch in Ontario has the authority to develop and provide these services but it is so understaffed and inadequately funded that its work is almost solely concerned with the immediate and urgent problems associated with the implementation of the Waste Management Act. Such is the state of the art in Canada.
The "art" is developing very rapidly in the United States and in other countries. Many new processes are being developed and the phenomena of solid waste generation and its implications are receiving considerable attention.
That is my point, and I will repeat the last sentence I quoted:
Many new processes are being developed and the phenomena of solid waste generation and its implications are receiving considerable attention.
Is this the position in Canada? My motion seems to be well accepted by members on both sides of the House. This is not a political matter, but one about which we should show deep concern to the point where members on the other side of the House are ready to make recommendations to the government, particularly with respect to the assistance that is required by municipalities and provincial governments to enable them to conduct more research into this problem. Then, at least we would not be waiting for conclusions to be reached by other jurisdictions in order that we could move into the area ourselves.
It has been stated that we are burying ourselves in our own garbage. I note, too, that an article has been written by Mr. Gordon Sutin entitled "The Case for Pulverization of Solid Wastes" printed in October, 1970 in "Public Works, City, County and State". I was impressed with what he had to say and, with the indulgence of my colleagues, I should like to quote as follows:
While incineration appears to offer the ultimate solution to the problem of disposing of solid wastes, it is a fact of life that many smaller communities cannot generate the capital to build the necessary facilities. This suggests, of course, that smaller communities should band together for the construction of one large regional incinerator, one plant to serve a number of municipalities. However, this again poses the problem of capital investment to establish and operate transfer stations.
What I am attempting to do this afternoon is to bring home the importance of the need for our continual involvement and appreciation of the problems of pollu-

March 6, 1972
Pollution
tion, which are increasing because of our increasing population, and because of the fact that many people, rather than saving things and using them over and over again, are now discarding all materials of consumption in an accelerated fashion. I should like to point to three recommendations which Messrs. Clark and Brown brought to the attention of the Ontario government. I do not think that we can differentiate between the jurisdictions because the problems that they have brought to our attention and on which they have made recommendations apply equally to the federal government. The first one reads as follows:
Immediate attention should be given to the co-ordination of the activities of all branches of the government concerned in the solid waste field, recognizing that integration of the processes to treat and dispose of these wastes might be achieved and that investigatory studies may have implications and benefits of common concern.
Another one reads:
Every attempt should be made to concentrate the research and development activities so as to provide for the eventual establishment of a centre for study and research.
One may think that this would be under the jurisdiction of the provincial government, but it is not in fact. I think we have a role to play in terms of leadership, money, research and assistance to municipalities and provinces.
Another important recommendation that was made is one which I hope the government has pursued in the past, and I hope we will hear about it from some members on the government side. It reads:
Data on the requirements, limitations and potentials of the various waste disposal systems should be made available to the public and to municipal officers on a continuing basis.
Another recommendation reads as follows:
Appropriate prototype facilities for a reclamation process should be established in such a location that the development of the process can be fostered and studied and under such conditions that the knowledge generated can be made readily available to all communities.
It seems to me that those recommendations can certainly be understood, accepted and implemented by the federal government, if in fact we are concerned about what is becoming a problem of ever increasing importance.
This is the third time that I have risen and spoken on this matter, and I will continue to do so. I know that the government has attempted to pay lip service to the motion that I have put forward on three occasions, but I do not think we have been doing enough. I think that pollution in all its aspects is an extremely serious problem. I am ready to accept that our young people are looking for answers to the various aspects of pollution which they find so unacceptable.

speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member for Sarnia-Lamb-ton (Mr. Cullen), who is the parliamentary secretary to some minister who is not quite doing his job, wants to be included. It is always nice to have his interjections.
In conclusion I would like to state that the over-all nature of the problem is such that attention should be drawn to it. I should like to point out two or three other recommendations on which I am sure the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton will wish to comment eventually so he might as well start writing now. Attention should be given to:
The improvement of organization and systemization of the waste material outflow portion of our consuming society,
The improvement of technology dealing with this outflow and with the separate steps of collecting, processing and disposing, and
The adoption of practices and policies that will close the loop between the materials consumption and the waste production parts of our society so that decisions relative to consumption will consider the waste product problem.
I do not think I can add any more at this time except to express the hope that when members rise to speak, particularly members on the other side, they will not turn this into a partisan issue since I did not until the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton interjected, but rather will offer some constructive criticisms and an appreciation of the intention behind this third attempt to bring this subject before the House for the consideration of hon. members.

subtopic: POLLUTION
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RESEARCH ON WASTE DISPOSAL METHODS
speechtext:
History may well record that the beginning of the decade of the seventies marked the turning point in man's use and abuse of the precious planet earth. In Cana'da, governments at all levels are becoming more and more aware that the biosphere is a closed system in which all things are recycled and re-used in support of the life process. Man, as a part of this closed life system, is dependent on it for his survival. Of all the living things, man alone is capable of consciously co-operating with nature to ensure his survival and progress.
Environmental modifications, which have accompanied our good yet shortsighted intentions of minimizing the spread of disease and maximizing the consumption of our raw resources, have had a global impact on human health and welfare. This has led our society to the discovery that we are dependent on, and part of, an ecosystem that we did not invent and must not destroy.
In this respect the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has given a very interesting, provocative and intelligent presentation to the House today. I commend him on his choice of subject matter. But as is usual, although the problems were raised, no suggestions for their solution were really presented. I intend to present what I believe are constructive suggestions that will help to solve the problems.
The hon. member suggested that we establish a research council of some kind, and that we spend many millions of dollars, at least that is what I believe it will cost, to gather civil servants and representatives of universities and industry together in such a research institute. I do not believe this would be an answer to the problem, for the simple reason that we live beside the

March 6, 1972

most powerful nation in the world, the most industrially advanced, and the most technologically advanced nation in the world.
I submit that there is a germ of a good idea in the speech made by the hon. member for Hamilton West, but I repeat that I do not think the real solution lies in establishing the kind of research institute he advocated. I believe we should be gathering information from the United States, a country which has many large, burgeoning cities that are coping with pollution problems. In this respect I think of the cities of Pittsburgh, Detroit and Buffalo. I believe we should ask them to share with us the knowhow that they are developing in solving these problems because they have more cash to work with, and more expertise available to them than we have. In addition, they have ten times as many people working on these problems as we could afford. I believe that at this stage we would be well advised to pick the best advice we can get from our great neighbour to the south, and I believe our great neighbour is ready to help us, particularly in light of our good relations with the United States.
I believe that we could send a small task force to the United States to gather information there. Pollution is a continental problem. The Americans are friendly to us when dealing with such matters. When presented with a joint problem such as we had during the Second World War, the Americans co-operated with us. They co-operated with us in the development of the St. Lawrence Seaway, and I am confident that thanks to the good neighbour policy that still exists between Canada and the United States, they will help us in coping with the enormous problem of pollution.
Canada has taken constructive action in attempting to clean up the Great Lakes, in co-operation with the United States. However, I believe we must extend our efforts to reach across the border and create dynamic dialogue, not only with congressmen, senators and mayors in the border states, but also with the people who reside along the Great Lakes in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, 1972 is the year that the great environmental conference is to be held in Stockholm. In my opinion, it is vital that Canadian views be expressed at all levels of contact with the United States of America, and dialogue should proceed immediately to achieve an exchange of views with people in Buffalo, Detroit and other large U S. cities, dialogue that will encompass people in Canadian cities like Toronto, Sarnia, Sudbury and Hamilton.
The Great Lakes can be saved for present use and for future generations. The time has come for instant and immediate discussions. I welcome the action taken by the federal government to date in substantially reducing pollution on the Canadian side of Lake Erie. The challenge now is not to attack the U.S. people but to persuade our giant neighbour to the south to take action at all levels of government, management, labour and the public. I believe that a conference attended by the heads of our two nations would be beneficial to this cause. I urge that serious consideration be given to the idea of establishing a system to curb pollution of the Great Lakes. I suggest that the International Joint Commission be given power, by international treaty, to recommend anti-pollution direc-
Pollution
tives, to be delivered and publicized to polluters on both sides of the border.
I believe in the principle that the polluter must pay. I also believe that on both sides of the border we have been lax in finding a means of sending the polluter a bill for payment, with the alternative of an injunction order backed up by international agreement to enforce such measures. This could all be worked out under the aegis of the International Joint Commission.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I was rather in despair during my first year as a member of the House of Commons. We questioned officials of the International Joint Commission who appeared before the Standing Committee on External Affairs when it was considering the estimates of the Commission. I gathered the impression from them that they did not want to rock the boat. I gathered the impression that they did not want to accept any real responsibility. They simply wanted to express opinions on how things could be changed, but they did not want the responsibility for cleaning up the Great Lakes. They did not want the responsibility of sending a bill to anyone for payment. I believe they should be engaged in drawing up a constructive program to stop this pollution. I want in some small way to accelerate the process because we simply cannot allow the pollution of the Great Lakes to continue.
I believe that when the United States finally gets around to doing something about the matter, it will proceed to do so very rapidly. I believe that our role should be that of a catalyst, pumping enthusiasm into the great nation to our south, discussing this question at all levels and all ages.
The greatest factor causing pollution in Hamilton harbour is waste from the city. The secondary stage of its sewage treatment system has been reached in Hamilton, thanks to co-operation at all levels of government. Part of this system has been paid for by federal funds. Once the system is fully developed, a great percentage of the pollution in Hamilton Bay will be removed for all time. Industry is partly responsible for the pollution, but industry is playing a large part in anti-pollution measures. Both the huge steel companies there, the Steel Company of Canada and the Dominion Foundries and Steel Company are spending vast sums of money on pollution control. I believe they should be encouraged.
Further, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary that all parties realize that the residents of Hamilton Beach must be protected from continuing pollution hazards. I am confident that they will soon see happier days with the possible development of park lands for the use of people in that immediate area.
In closing I reiterate that the hon. member for Hamilton West has raised an extremely interesting matter. I think he was deficient in presenting solutions. I think the Canadian role today should be that of a catalyst, to inspire and work with the Americans in bringing about reforms in the field of pollution.

subtopic: POLLUTION
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RESEARCH ON WASTE DISPOSAL METHODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the notice of motion before the House is a good one. It deals with a request to set up more research facilities in Canada in an effort to overcome some of the severe pollu-

March 6, 1972
Pollution
tion problems facing the nation. Although we are able to discuss only briefly some of the many things which ought to be done to remedy this situation, I nevertheless am pleased because the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has brought this matter before the House and thereby has given us an opportunity to say publicly a few words on it.
To begin with, I presume that the motion is drafted in its present language because not sufficient research has been done in Canada or any other nation along the lines suggested by the motion. I could not agree more with that presumption, Mr. Speaker. Here we are, asking for a research development program to be set up with definite guidelines. In that connection may I say that my party has for a long time proposed the setting up of an environmental council of Canada. Such an environmental council should, in my view, be established along the lines of the Economic Council of Canada. They would be non-political. We would pick some of the most able people in Canada to sit on the council. They would report to Canada-every year, I presume-and outline the environmental problems which Canadians should meet. They would criticize, if necessary, any lack of program or policy on the part of the federal or provincial government-those governments which are supposed to be taking care of this problem.
I suggest that the need for research in Canada is urgent, just as it is in many nations of the world. A large number of articles and books have been written by people trained in this field. Some of them are biologists who have spent their lives studying the food chain, and so on, and they have indicated that we cannot continue along the lines we are following today and that we must take drastic action. Mr. Speaker, the proper action must be devised by those who have the expertise and training necessary to give us guidance in this field.
The notice of motion mentions solid-waste disposal. Although there is a host of pollutants in the world, I should like to deal briefly with solid-waste disposal and demonstrate the need for a plan to recycle all these solid wastes so that we can obtain from what is now waste material minerals and other materials which will assist in the industrial processes of the future. May I point something out before I go any further. I believe that three factors are invariably involved in research into pollution. One of those is population, the other resource development, and the third, of course, pollution itself. You cannot separate those factors, Mr. Speaker.
Canada, in common with other nations, will in the near future need to formulate a population control program. We must sit down and discover what will happen if the world in which we live becomes overpopulated. Information currently available tells me that by the year 2000, which is just 28 years from 1972, the population of this world will double. What will this mean? It means this: If the population doubles, the volume of material goods which the people of the world will need will also double. We shall need many more motor cars, colleges, schools, doctors, and so on. Vastly increased amounts of raw material will be dug out from our store-house of treasure in the earth, a store-house which the world holds, if the burgeoning population is to maintain standards of living
that we currently enjoy. Many say that we cannot indefinitely go on as at present: there is a limit to how much food we can raise in the world and to the resources which can be made available for the use of individuals. Before we reach this limit, what must we do? First, I think all countries of the world, perhaps through the United Nations, will have to set out some kind of population policy and try to stabilize world population through a host of processes which I will not go into now.
If I may return to the subject of minerals, Mr. Speaker, a number of minerals throughout the globe are already in short supply. So far no plan has been made by Canada or by any country of the world, that I know of, to ration the mineral resources of this world so that those who come after us will have something to use. So far, nothing has been done to establish a program for reclaiming certain waste materials. This notice of motion suggests that more research be applied to the subject we are considering so that we may return to the economy-return to society, if you like-many minerals which today are wasted. I could think of all kinds of garbage dumps where minerals are being wasted. Commodities made of minerals are just thrown to one side, covered over with dirt, and left. Sometimes they are dumped in the ocean or the lakes and are destroyed.
Not only Canada and the United States, but other nations of the world are conducting research into this question in an effort to determine which materials can be recycled. We can all learn from these efforts and we should pool all this knowledge and the results of research. Perhaps an agency for receiving and disseminating knowledge in this field should be set up through the United Nations.
This spring, Mr. Speaker, there is to be a meeting in Sweden sponsored by the United Nations. All nations belonging to the UN organization will be invited to look into the problem we are now discussing-pollution and its effect on the ocean, air and life in general. I therefore hope that we will devise a plan of action for undertaking the necessary research in this field in order that we may solve the problem of solid-waste disposal and attempt to put most wasted materials back into use.
To show the seriousness of the problem, may I quote a few figures. It is useless ducking our heads in the sand and saying that eventually, if we dump wastes and solids somewhere, nature will look after them and break them down into their original elements. This will not happen, for pollution has become too serious a problem in Canada and every other nation of the world. The survey I am about to refer to was made in 1969. One might say that a survey taken two years ago was taken long ago, and so it was. Nevertheless, the situation is even worse now, simply because the so-called standard of living of people is rising rapidly. We have reached the stage where people can buy goods in containers that can be thrown away or discarded. This just adds to our pollution problem.
In this article they stated that the experts felt the problem of pollution and recycling required a radical change in patterns of consumption and disposal. I do not think anyone in this House would disagree with that statement.

March 6, 1972

They stated they checked with a number of large cities in the United States. Time does not permit me to give all the data. However, this is very interesting and is something which I think closely parallels the Canadian way of life. In talking about the United States, they said:
Every man, woman and child in the country, on average is now generating more than five pounds of refuse a day-household, commercial, and industrial ... but excluding ... agricultural waste.
We find that in 1969-two years ago-every individual in the United States had every day of his life five pounds of refuse credited to him. When you multiply that by the over 200 million people in the United States, it represents a vast tonnage of refuse per year that has to be thrown away. The problem has become almost insurmountable in so far as municipalities and local agencies are concerned. Again talking about the United States, the waste includes, and I quote:
That adds up to more than a ton per person per year ... It includes 30 million tons of paper, more than 4 million tons of plastic, 48 billion cans and 26 billions bottles and jars.
That is what they are trying to get rid of each and every year in the United States. The problem of pollution has become so immense that it is no wonder there is talk about recycling. The article continues:
Collection and disposal facilities already are staggering under the load, which is increasing rapidly.
"The major metropolitan areas are standing in front of an avalanche" .. . and it's threatening to bury them."
The article points out that some of the larger cities are now planning to carry their refuse by train hundreds of miles away from the city centres. In fact, one city is planning to haul the garbage over 250 miles by train and dumping it in a desert area away from the burgeoning populations of the future. All they are doing is transferring the problem from one area to another. The answer to this question is not to take the refuge and dump it on somebody else's doorstep or in another area, although this might stall the problem for a short period of time. The answer is to find some method of recycling all the materials we have. This would be achieved by the type of research which the hon. member for Hamilton West indicates in his motion.
There is much more I would like to talk about, but the time allotted to me is running out. I am certain other hon. members want to speak on this subject. In conclusion, I would like to say that one of the weaknesses of this administration-and I might say that this is political-is that we have never had an environmental policy put to this House or the people of Canada. We need this type of policy. We must know what we intend to do about pollution. What shall we do about resource development, population, and management in the future? What are the plans for development of urban areas? Shall we concentrate more and more on the bigger cities and bypass other areas of Canada? If the plan is to set up a mid-Canada corridor or create cities and industries outside the current, large urban centres, now is the time to do it.
We have not had such a prediction from this government. At no time has there been an environmental policy concerning what we shall do and how we will conserve our resources. I add to the motion that I think research
Pollution
can solve this problem and at least give us a goal or goals toward which the municipalities, provinces and the federal government can aim in the years ahead.

subtopic: POLLUTION

speechtext:
The hon. member may have a lot more time after the next election to be worried about the situation in Hamilton and to be a little more parochial. I do not think anyone can argue with the position put forward by the hon. member. The point he is trying to make is good. However, I would have liked him to have zeroed in on one area. In the limited time we have, it is impossible for him or any member of this House to do justice to this motion.
The disposal of solid waste is one of the great problems that faces each municipality, province and Canada as a whole. On a more parochial level, there were two gentlemen who did not wait for government grants or initiative. They saw the problem locally and decided to do something about it. The problem was the disposal of solid chemical waste. Mr. Stanley and Mr. Harry Goodfellow tried to find some method of disposing of chemical waste. They were successful.
When the hon. member for Hamilton West talks about coming up with something that is not only good for the standpoint of pollution control but economically feasible, he makes a good point.
The gentlemen to whom I have referred formed a corporation called Goodfellow Enterprises. Subsequently, Canadian Industries Limited looked into this project, saw that it was good and would be a money-maker. They recently purchased this company and will be getting into this field. It is that kind of initiative that has made Canada great-not the handing out of government loans and government grants all the time, but seeing the problem and doing something about it.
I have done a fair amount of research on this subject. One always hesitates to put forward his views because I am sure the hon. member will agree that when you rise in the House of Commons to talk about pollution control the tendency is to say, "No wonder he talks about this: he is from Sarnia," or, "from Hamilton." In this way we give our communities a bad name which they do not deserve, whereas in point of fact we can see the problem developing and are trying to nip it in the bud. In Sarnia we welcomed the Lambton Industrial Society which is look-

March 6, 1972
Pollution
ing into all areas of pollution. They endeavoured to put their collective brains together to see if there was some way in this area to cut down air pollution caused by coal burning which has a higher sulphur content.
There are four general categories of solid waste- municipal, industrial, agricultural and mineral. It is my impression that major studies have been concerned primarily with municipal waste, the refuse produced by households and commerce which eventually finds its way to the public dump. Because this waste is so visible, attention is focused on it and other wastes do not receive the same measure of attention. However, it should be noted that in terms of tonnage, mining and industrial waste is astronomical by comparison with municipal waste. For example, in Canada in 1970, mining operations produced 440 million tons of solid waste, and agricultural waste totalled 150 million tons. Municipal waste accounted for only 17 million tons during the same period. I use the word "only" because of the huge amounts produced by other sources.
Municipal solid waste-garbage, in plain language-is anything that is deposited in a garbage can and a good many items that are not. It includes, in addition to everyday refuse such as potato-peelings, paper, rags, packages and old clothing, items such as junk furniture, worn out appliances, the refuse of industry and the debris from construction projects. Attempts recently have been made in Ottawa to recycle the discarded paper which accumulates in household waste. I hope they continue and that they will prove successful, because while the composition of refuse by weight varies from city to city, a typical Canadian or American municipal refuse accumulation contains 59 per cent paper. The remainder would be in roughly the following proportions: 10 per cent wood, lawn and garden waste; 9 per cent food waste; 8.5 per cent glass, other ceramics and ash; 7.5 per cent metal and 6 per cent clothes, rags, plastic, rubber and leather.
The hon. member who spoke before me suggested we should explore more vigorously the possibilities of deriving some benefit from waste. We might, for instance, find some use for tailings which are piled up around mining communities. Perhaps we could find a way of getting iron out of the slag dumps. This can be done at the present time but it is not feasible from an economic point of view. It is not right to suggest that no research work is carried out in this field. Before the war, research was being carried out in this connection, to my personal knowledge.
Who generates municipal waste? Everyone is responsible for generating refuse. It is produced constantly, day in and day out. It is produced by office workers, homemakers, factory workers, shopkeepers, farmers-virtually by everybody. The affluent produce more trash than the poor. The amount of garbage generated by Canadians in 1970 averaged 4.3 lbs. per person per day, a total of 1,580 lbs. per person per year. It is estimated that the average United States citizen generates 1,800 lbs. of solid waste per year, while in backward India the figure is about 200 lbs. Generally, everyday household trash goes into the garbage can for collection by the city through the agency of private sanitation companies. Business and industry usually arrange for a special refuse removal at their own
[Mr. Cullen.J
expense. Regardless of how or where it is produced, virtually all refuse ends up as land-fill or in the incinerator.
It has been suggested, and the motion before us suggests, that the problem of dealing effectively with solid waste has now reached crisis proportions. Even if this is not the case at the moment, the stark statistic introduced by the hon. member who preceded me, namely, that the world's population will double by the year 2,000, is enough to convince anyone that the time to begin working very hard to eliminate the pollution threat through recycling and other means, is now.

We are not faced with a sudden crisis. Garbage has been around as long as mankind, ever since the Stone Age. The difficulty is that in the more congested, more sophisticated societies, it is not so easy to avoid the problems it creates. We cannot avoid it or walk away from it. Some time ago members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development had an opportunity to visit an Indian community which was established in the Northwest Territories at about the turn of the century. As a result of the build-up of hunting and household wastes during all those years, a pollution situation had developed. The department concluded that the population of the village ought to be moved from that particular site and consultation began with the Indians to see how their removal from this unhealthy site could best be arranged.
So it is not only modern cities which build up pollution through an accumulation of household waste. In times gone by it was possible for communities simply to walk away and find new sites for their homes. But this is no solution for people living in cities like Sarnia, Hamilton or Madawaska?
Recognizing we are faced with a problem we must act as all Liberal governments have acted, that is, we must devise satisfactory solutions. And the present government has come up with some splendid solutions-the clean air act and the clean water act, to name two examples. Some people say they are not enough-but they are important steps forward. I, personally, would like to see the International Joint Commission be given more money and greater power so that it could do what needs to be done to clean up the Great Lakes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying prior to private members' hour, the whole question of containerization in air transportation has, in my opinion, an increasing role to play. We were talking about cargo containers and I should also like to speak of the possibility of passenger luggage containerization which might be developed within similar parameters. In either case, the object would be to load cargo and/or passengers in a container and an aircraft according to their ultimate destination. Thus, a container for Montreal, Toronto or other points serviced by the central airport facility could be loaded on the same aircraft but quickly unloaded on to the ground transit vehicle with the minimum of handling for the balance of the journey. Packaging passengers in that way may sound somewhat inhuman, but we are thinking of larger units, which might be a whole vehicle or aircraft, or a significant portion of it.
It can be seen that such a system could eliminate a number of costly and time-consuming steps in any long air journey. It would seem logically to follow that the ground vehicle, or a section of it, would be stationed immediately adjacent to the unloading aircraft and simply joined to the main line track, or other right of way hopefully going in the right direction. As the major part of the initial system would parallel the St. Lawrence Seaway, further possibilities for integration with water transport exist. This is in addition to the availability of
CNR and Air Canada
fresh water for the industry and population to be served by this industrial transportation corridor.
Such a centrally located facility would immediately serve smaller cities whose travellers must presently find their way to cities served by major airports. For longer journeys they would have the Kingston airport, and for shorter journeys they would have the surface transport to the airports handling short and medium haul flights. It should take more than a footnote to indicate that the ground transit would have to be tied into the existing airports for connecting short-haul passengers and cargo.
The addition of tie lines to the ground transit system would be logical even in the early states. The most obvious tie-in would be the nation's capital, not only providing it with better air service but, again, eliminating a significant amount of short-haul air traffic between Ottawa-Hull and the country's two largest cities, Toronto and Montreal. This should reduce air traffic movement, according to my figures, by a further 5 per cent in Toronto and 6 per cent in Montreal, at today's rates. Communities such as Belleville, Brockville and Valleyfield would be served by the main line. Cities such as Peterborough could be conveniently tied in by a number of alternative methods. Northern New York state cities, such as Rochester and Syracuse, could be serviced by hovercraft or hydrofoil vehicles.
A natural extension of the ground service would be to cities such as Quebec and Windsor,serving intermediate points such as Trois-Rivieres, Sorel, Hamilton, Kitchener and London. This would service existing population and industry and encourage the economic growth of regions now not economically or conveniently accessible. It would create an industrial corridor extending some 750 miles with convenient interchanges of people, industrial components and goods.
Ultimately further tie-lines could be extended to regions such as Lac Ste. Jean and the eastern townships, and northward from Toronto as far as Sudbury, allowing commercial access as well as providing a transportation system which would take people from the crowded urban centres to some of the most beautiful recreation areas in the country.
I previously mentioned that time rather than distance is the key factor in transportation of people. With highspeed surface transport, people could enjoy the benefits of country or smaller town living while being able to work in the major cities. This provides a better life style for some while at the same time taking the pressure for growth off the already strangling large urban communities. One could conveniently live in Cobourg, Ontario, and work in Toronto. With a northern line one could live in his year-round home on Lake Simcoe, or even in Muskoka, while one's means of livelihood was in Toronto. I am sure similar examples could be drawn for Montrealers.
It has been estimated that a major airport requires a community of 100,000 to 150,000 people to service it. I notice that these are just about the figures being used in conjunction with the new Toronto region airport. This includes not just those employed at the airport but their families and the multiplicity of services they require, such as shopkeepers, barbers, travellers, doctors and lawyers, plus the recreational and administrative needs of all.

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
Existing centres would develop, but it may also be necessary or desirable to inaugurate new planned communities, perhaps 25 or more miles east and west of the airport site enabling airport personnel to commute in minutes-a great opportunity for the planning genius of a Buckminster Fuller or a Moshe Safde or any number of excellent Canadian planners!
One of the key considerations would be air and noise pollution. This factor is one that makes the Kingston region a logical one, assuming that the facility is not immediately adjacent to Kingston. It is likely that any major housing development within a 10 to 25-mile radius of the airport would be forbidden. An extension of this would be expropriation of land and the establishment of a national park or wilderness area. This provides an apparent contradiction because one would hardly think of a wilderness area beset by air and noise pollution.
Normal traffic patterns would have considerable bearing on the land use. Industrial development could be quite satisfactory, even complementary in some areas. Other areas might prove quite suitable for wildlife, while others for camping. Considerations for permanent living are quite different from those for industrial or occasional use. The need for nature preserves and lands for recreational use will grow, as does population and leisure time. Not all will choose to live in less dense areas and commute. Even if such an area were to serve just the Kingston region, the growth of that city as the hub of the transportation network would be sufficient justification.
I mentioned previously that the ground transit would have to connect with existing airports serving Toronto and Montreal. In so far as passengers are concerned, there may be a case made for interconnecting air shuttle service. Similar services may be provided for other communities, particularly those not served by the ground transit system. Canada's STOL development might well provide the proper type of aircraft for such service.
It is further possible that traffic volumes might justify interconnecting flight schedules with other major cities in the medium haul range, such as Winnipeg and Halifax. These services would apply to incoming and departing long-range, international and transcontinental flights of the Los Angeles-Kingston type.
Frequency of schedules for the surface transit is an essentia] factor. All of the time advantage could be lost if infrequency of schedules required passengers to take the "ten o'clock", arriving at 11 to catch a noon or 1 p.m. flight. Conversely the arriving passenger might have to wait an hour or more for a departing train or unit. The growth of the corridor would ultimately justify frequent arrivals and departures, but any frequency which could require waiting periods of an hour or more would seriously impair the total concept.
Technology, again, can provide the answer to this problem. Smaller groupings of surface vehicles can provide part of the answer. Economic, self-propelled modules are another possibility. Perhaps the best solution is a continuing or perpetual power source into which the module or unit is connected with schedules and the number of

modules in a transit unit is contingent upon demand. But this is another problem for the scientists, Mr. Speaker.
As one thinks in terms of the emphasis Canada should give in the areas of science policy, research and development, it would seem natural that transportation should rate high on any list of priorities. There is no reason, however, why we should have any natural advantages, in spite of the fact that we have natural potential and problems. Without a project to give focus and thrust, as well as market, we could wander in the never-never land of unapplied research. This project would be the catalyst for a national scientific effort which could have significant international market potential.
An international centre for transportation studies could be established, perhaps at Queen's University in Kingston. Other Canadian universities could be participants covering specific areas of concentration. At the same time, international dimension could be provided by encouraging visiting specialists from other countries to participate. Not only would we achieve the results of research, but we could also train specialists to administer our transportation systems.
The broader aspects of transportation should be intertwined-the sociological ramifications, the industrial development, urban styles and the unifying effects on a nation so diverse in all its aspects. The economic consequences could be substantial, resulting in the sale of technology and much of our hardware abroad.
The regional economic benefits are obvious-efficient transport of goods within a major market; components from a tool shop in Windsor delivered rapidly to the major assembly plant in Sorel or Quebec city; greater mobility of labour; a direct tie-in to the automotive heartland of the Detroit area and adjacent to the Boston, Washington, Chicago triangle, the largest market concentration in the U.S. and perhaps the world.
The project itself develops its own market. The rolling stock, containers, the switchgear and complex electronic systems all feed high technology, labour-intensive Canadian industry. With developed know-how we would have immense export potential in a field in which we could be pre-eminent. Examples of subsidiary economic benefits are virtually endless.
Mr. Speaker, you might ask about the cost of such an operation. That is difficult to project but I think there are certain trade-offs. This is of greater value to eastern Canada than the economic well-being of western Canada. Western Canada might ask, what is in it for us? I would suggest any improvement in our transportation system and the economy in any part of the country is good for all parts of the country. I would suggest that we also think of pipelines for gas and oil to serve our eastern markets. There are those who ask why we should spend more money for western oil or gas when we can bring in offshore or foreign product? Well, Mr. Speaker, I think this is part of the price of belonging to the club, part of the price of being Canadian. For many years westerners have paid a higher price for consumer goods produced in the eastern industrial centres in order to protect the economy of eastern Canada and this, in turn, helped them. It works both ways, and I think this is the trade-off. I do not know
March 6, 1972

what the cost would be-say about $100 billion. No one can argue with those figures.
