speechtext:
Whatever the cost, it would certainly be outweighted by the benefits and would be substantially less than the ultimate cost of laissez-faire development or lack of purpose. This is the greatest danger we face.
The Kingston airport itself is not the key to the whole concept. I think it is a major component in a vital plan. The whole transit system is important and I think the Kingston airport could be the cornerstone.
All this came up, Mr. Speaker, because of the subject of our debate and the recent announcement of the major airport which will take up a large segment of my constituency. I mentioned the effects on my constituency earlier, which are not all pleasant, but this is the price of what I guess we call progress, or a type of progress. The economic benefits for my region are considerable, but many of my constituents are concerned about the possible selling price of their homes. However, past experience indicates that this price rises in such circumstances. There is a tremendous amount of economic fall-out from an airport facility-new industry, new job opportunities, new business opportunities and excellent transportation, so the cost of existing properties should increase.
But that is not my sole criteria, Mr. Speaker. The economic benefits are great but I think we should consider the human benefits, particularly as we talk of the longterm. I like to think what might have been decided 20 or 30 years ago if politicians then had been talking about the type of future, the type of cities, the transportation networks which we would require today. In its initial stages, I think this is the type of thing that could be a priority task for the recently established Institute of Public Policy Research. This may be the sort of thing it is designed for- to look well into the future and do the type of forward thinking for which we in this chamber do not have time. Regrettably, our system is reactionary-we react to events, political pressures and economic pressures. But the Institute of Public Policy Research is a non-partisan vehicle supported by all levels of government and the private sector. It should be able to look at long-range goals and perhaps give guidance to politicians like ourselves so that we may more realistically base our policy.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I hope that what I have suggested will be raised in committee with the officials of the railways, the airlines and the various departments involved. Now that we have made the decision for current needs for the next 20 or 30 years, for the next generation, it is time to start thinking beyond those years because the potential for our country is considerable. If we are wise now and look ahead, our children and grandchildren will thank us-but if we do not, they will damn us as some damn our forefathers today.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the interest in this bill, which is perennial, is about proportionate to the influence of what we say during the course of this debate to the CN and its operations in the next year. As a matter of fact, I know of no other Crown
CNR and Air Canada
corporation or agency responsible to this Parliament which is less responsive to the wishes or the influence of Parliament than is Canadian National Railways.
However, we nevertheless welcome the opportunity provided us every year through the vehicle of this financing bill to place on record our views and grievances. I come from a province which perhaps-yes, without a doubt-is more dependent upon Canadian National Railways and the services of CN than any other province in Canada. We are totally dependent upon CN both from the point of view of Air Canada and the service provided to our province by Air Canada and the ground service provided to us through the railways and the ferry services operated by CN.
Just about three years ago Canadian National was permitted to suspend rail passenger service in Newfoundland as a consequence of an application placed before the Canadian Transport Commission. I refer to the order of the CTC of July 3, 1968, No. R.2673, which gave authority to Canadian National Railways to discontinue its rail passenger service in the province of Newfoundland. Since that time our province has been without rail passenger service, the only province in the country so deprived. Consequently, we have to suffer the shortcomings of what is at best a most inadequate public transportation system.
Perhaps this is the most opportune time-indeed it will probably be the only opportunity we will have in the course of this Parliament-to review what has transpired since that decision of the Canadian Transport Commission of July 3, 1968. I would point out that I was very happy to join my colleagues in the submission to the CTC dated February 15, 1972, in which we asked the commission to reconsider its order of July 3, 1968, permitting CN to withdraw rail passenger service in Newfoundland. Our reason for doing so was prompted by a decision of the commission on February 8, 1972, in which it issued a decision requiring the railways, CN and CP, to continue operating rail passenger services between Montreal and the maritime provinces. The railways had applied to the commission for permission to withdraw this particular rail passenger service, which included the main line operations between St. John's, Moncton, Halifax, Sydney and Montreal as well as the various connecting services to the maritime points and the Gaspe regions of Quebec. The commission, in its release announcing that decision, said: Cost studies carried out by the commission in connection with the February 8 decision identified a total actual loss on these services of $14,834,298 in 1970. Under the law, the services now are eligible for federal subsidies of up to 80 per cent of annual losses. At the 1970 level, this could cost the taxpayers almost $12 million a year or $1 million a month.
I can think of no better way than to continue quoting from the release of the commission:
The decision, by the Railway Transport Committee, saw no evidence that the services could be rendered profitable with current schedules, operating practices and equipment. It added: "Hence, given the actual losses incurred and the demands and traffic patterns, the committee is of the opinion that it is possible through imaginative improvements to develop a maritimes passenger-train system which will satisfy the needs of the travelling public and, at the same time, justify whatever cost there may be to the federal treasury.
In this decision the committee identifies the basic rail passenger network as it presently exists in the Atlantic region east of Mont-

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
real. Pending the achievement of its objective as just stated, the committee determines that all the passenger-train services under consideration should not be discontinued. As time goes on, and suggestions or proposals for improvement are analyzed and accepted by the committee, it may be necessary to require alterations in the services as presently operated, having regard to the needs of the travelling public and the cost to the Canadian taxpayers".
That is the end of the quotation which in effect is the judgment of the commission in response to the application by the two railways to discontinue the service between Montreal and the Maritime provinces. As I indicated, this rather momentous decision by the commission prompted the submission my colleagues and I made to the commission on February 15, 1972, to which I shall refer in a moment. I should like to quote from this release because I think it is very relevant to my remarks. The committee stated in its release:
In order to ensure that all possible methods of improvement are considered, the commission invites suggestions from the public. Such suggestions, dealing with mainline or local aspects of the services, should be submitted in writing-
Then the address is given to which one should write. Persons making submission are asked to give consideration to the following points:
1.	Routing, including possible combinations of service on CNR and CP Rail lines.
2.	Frequency of service on the resulting route or routes, with possible variations in summer and winter schedules.
3.	Train departure-arrival times.
4.	Connecting services by rail, road, air and water.
5.	Methods and costs of providing meals.
6.	Methods and costs of providing sleeping car service.
7.	Fare levels for coach services.
8.	Improved reservation procedures to reduce the "no show" problem.
The commission hopes to obtain responses from the appropriate departments of provincial and municipal governments, the railways, trade unions, travel agencies, public bodies and individual citizens. It is particularly interested in the views of those members of the public who have actually travelled on the trains in the last two years.
We fee] that the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission is very relevant to the arguments we have placed before the House since the commission in its judgment of July 3, 1968, allowed by its order No. R. 2673 Canadian National to discontinue railway passenger service in Newfoundland, hence depriving our province of a total, comprehensive public transportation system.
Now I should like to quote from the submission of the Newfoundland members of parliament to the commission, of February 15, 1972, which reads in part as follows:
We submit that the bus service provided by Canadian National as an alternative to the train service does not now, and probably will never, fulfil the needs of the travelling public. Service has been anything but adequate; even more alarming, service is less than safe-as statistics recording the number of accidents will attest.
My colleagues and I will present arguments to support that contention during the course of this debate. Our submission continues:
0- ofCN's own vice-presidents, J. A. McDonald, has said publicly that "anyone who has experienced the miseries of peak 
congestion on even the most modern 12-lane super highway will recognize that road transport is incapable of providing adequately for all the needs of the travelling public". In Newfoundland, we have no 12-lane super highway: it is a two-lane, and the miseries and agonies of travelling by bus along the nearly 600 miles can be documented at length.
My colleagues and I will attempt to do just that-document our case in this respect. We feel that the poor service in Newfoundland during the past three years-the "road cruiser service" as CN styles it-is totally inadequate to meet the needs of the travelling public. Buses are uncomfortable and less than safe. In fact, they do not meet the demands of the public travelling over such long distances in order to make necessary connections with the mainland transportation system.
Why have we arrived at the state where we have an inadequate bus service which is supposed to be superior to the rail passenger service which it was to improve? It is a fact, as we have indicated during past debates on bills similar to this, that the CN deliberately set out in Newfoundland to downgrade the passenger service so that patronage would fall off to the point where they could successfully file an application with the commission pointing out that the service was no longer being patronized to an extent to justify continuing the service and that the operating deficit was increasing to the point where CN felt that it was no longer able to carry on.
They took a five-year trial period for purposes of their application. During that five-year period they took one year by their own accounting procedures which are incomprehensible to most people. They were able to show that the rail passenger service in Newfoundland for that particular year operated at a deficit of $900,000. Yet, the service in the maritime provinces is going to cost $1 million a month, whereas our service for the entire province during its most difficult year was only able to arrive at a maximum deficit of $900,000. Service was downgraded and deliberately slow. There can be no doubt about that. It was downgraded to the point where patronage fell off and where, as I have said, they were able to successfully appeal to the commission through the collusion of the then provincial government-and, I might say, the collu-1 sion of the Canadian Transport Commission and the government of Canada-and argue a case for the discontinuance of rail passenger service. Presumably they were able to satisfy the commission that a bus system in Newfoundland would not only meet the needs of the travelling public but would also be more economical to operate.
What is the case? For the year 1970-71 the bus service in Newfoundland, the CN road cruiser service, operated at a deficit of $400,000, plus considerable inconvenience and discomfort to the travelling public the like of which was never known during the days of the rail passenger service. What about the safety feature of this new bus system? I will not say too much about that because my colleagues, the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) and the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle) who represent constituents who are much more familiar with the bus service than I am, will I am sure outline the unsatisfactory safety record. Suffice to say, however, that there is growing concern in the province of Newfoundland among the travelling public
March 6, 1972

about the growing number of accidents involving the CN road cruisers.
The inadequacy of the system was dramatically underlined and sharply driven home during the recent strike of the air traffic controllers. The province of Newfoundland which, as I said, is totally dependent upon CN services, found itself totally dependent upon the CN road cruiser service for connections with the mainland. The people had to try the bus service because no other alternative was left open to them, and they found out for themselves the discomfort, indeed the hazards, of travelling across the 600 miles of Trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland to get to the mainland via this means.
We believe that the time has now come when the government agents, the Canadian Transport Commission, should reconsider the decision that it took in July of 1968 in light of the operating experience of the past three years. If they do that in an objective way by having public hearings, calling witnesses and having the kind of examination of the service which will bring out the facts, we believe that in fairness they can only come to the conclusion that they erred in their decision of July, 1968, in allowing Canadian National to discontinue rail passenger service in the province of Newfoundland.
I am not arguing for a return of the system, as we knew it, for a return of the Newfie "Bullet" of fame, but I do suggest that since we do have an inadequate system and we are totally dependent on this road cruiser service operated by the CN monopoly in Newfoundland-since this service is operating at a substantial deficit which is increasing and, I submit, at a considerable inconvenience to the public-the time has now come when it is incumbent upon the government to consider the advisability of providing the province of Newfoundland with standard gauge rails.
I realize that this is something that should have been done 22 years ago when Newfoundland became a province of Canada. But it was not done then. I think a case can be made for it now. What better way could there be for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which is so involved in substantial expenditures in Newfoundland, to provide a so-called infrastructure? What better could it do than provide funds whereby Canadian National and the government of Canada would standardize the rail lines in Newfoundland to link us with the rail network of North America? This would make eminently more sense than some of the infrastructure expenditures that have been undertaken by that department during the past two years. It would have the effect of making transportation to Newfoundland considerably more economical than at present.
In the first instance, it would provide the people of Newfoundland with a direct connection with the rail lines of the continent for passenger service. And, probably even more important, it would provide the province of Newfoundland with a direct link with the continental rail network for the purpose of freight transportation, which is so important to my province which is totally dependent upon imports of consumer goods from the mainland of Canada. We feel there is a case to be made for such an
CNR and Air Canada
expenditure by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
I regret that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) is not present for this debate. I am sure he has a very good reason for being elsewhere, but the fact remains that he is not here, able to hear or respond to the arguments presented by hon. members during the course of this debate. Hopefully, we will have another opportunity to present these arguments and to question the minister during committee stage of the bill.
I feel we should now take a long, hard look at the situation in Newfoundland with regard to Canadian National. I believe it is difficult, if not impossible, to justify CN bus service in the province of Newfoundland which is unable to meet the demands of the travelling public and must operate at a growing annual deficit.
As I indicated at the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, we are short-changed in that we do not have adequate public transportation service in the province of Newfoundland but have inadequate transportation service which hampers resource development. It also hampers tourist development and causes considerably inconvenience to the travelling public. For these reasons alone a case can be made for reopening the whole application and the whole area of the decision which was made by the commission in 1968. In this respect it might be advantageous to quote from the MacPherson commission report. This commission made its report in 1961 but it is the only report we have. We feel it is still relevant. As recorded at page 72, volume I, the commission stated:
Locational and resource disadvantages are well known in Canada. Remedies for overcoming them have been built into national policy. Transportation has been used as one instrument for mitigating locational disadvantage . . . Locational disadvantages can still be ameliorated by national transportation policies.
I do not think that we have a national transportation policy. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Danson) referred to this question during the course of his remarks. I think the way he put it was that there is need for a more integrated transportation policy. The leader of the NDP made the same point during the course of his remarks, which I substantially support. We can refer to the recommendations of the MacPherson commission as supporting argument for our contention. But there are also other data which will support our argument. If transportation in Canada is to make sense, then transportation decisions, as the leader of the NDP said, will have to be made on the basis of public need and not on the basis of political expediency.
It was political expediency that brought about the decision of the commission, in the first instance, which allowed CN to withdraw railway passenger service from the province of Newfoundland. Decisions should not be made on the basis of some sort of simplistic approach, the kind of simplistic approach advocated by the Minister of Transport. It is interesting to examine what he said before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications at its hearings on February 25, 1971, dealing with this matter. He said:
Where it is feasible it is still the objective of the ministry to provide services on a cost-recovery basis to the maximum extent possible.

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
If we are to have a transportation policy based on that philosophy, then it is my contention that the people of Canada will be shortchanged. It is my contention that if we are to have a public transportation policy based on a pay-as-you-go philosophy, then we will not have an adequate transportation system in this country. Certainly the facts, as I have tried to lay them on the record, indicate that this is so in Newfoundland today, because the arguments used to support the decision to disallow rail service in Newfoundland were purely on the basis of cost-recovery or on the basis of operating deficits.
No public transportation service can operate on a break-even basis, let alone a profitable basis. The public will have to underwrite the cost of public transportation. It seems to me that the difficulties we are experiencing are a direct consequence of the attitude of the government of Canada and of the Minister of Transport, whose philosophy I have tried to outline in the quotation I have given. The minister would be well advised to heed the words of his cabinet colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Development (Mr. Marchand) who, when he was president of the Confederation of National Trade Unions in 1961, said:
transportation policy is closely tied to economic planning and as such must be linked to the common good and not the profitability of private enterprise.
Public transportation must flow from a direct, integrated government policy on transportation. We do not seem to get that from the government. I submit that until we have a definition of the government's policy on transportation, we will have this ad hoc, hit or miss attitude of the Canadian Transport Commission carrying out what they interpret to be the philosophy of the government of the day. We need only add that until we have such an integrated and adequate transportation policy from the government we will continue to have conflicting decisions by the commission which, under the scrutiny of examination, make no sense at all.
Therefore I appeal to the government, and in particular to the Minister of Transport, to enter into discussions with the president of the CTC with a view to at least having public hearings into the service provided by Canadian National in Newfoundland since the momentous decision of the commission in July, 1968, by which it allowed Canadian National to withdraw from railway passenger service in the province. Such an examination in my view, Mr. Speaker, can lead only to the conclusion that Newfoundland is inadequately served by the public transportation system of this country. That inadequacy must be met by this government. We feel it can only be met by serious consideration being given to providing the necessary funds whereby the province of Newfoundland, in keeping with the latest technology, can adopt the standard, gaugerail line. That would at least link us with the continental rail network and thus give us half a chance to get goods in and out of the province and provide our people with decent rail service.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us is one in which Parliament is being asked to vote money for the Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. Naturally, the debate on this

bill becomes one in which Members of Parliament state their views as to improvements in various areas that ought to be made by both these transport agencies.
The leader of this party, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) spoke this afternoon in a general way, indicating our view with respect to transport policy in a broad sense. He also said that a number of us in this party would be dealing, one by one, with specific issues. I intend to confine my remarks, therefore, to the matter of further improvements that must be made with respect to the pensions of the Canadian National Railways. I am very conscious that a little over one year ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) stood in his place in this House and announced a significant and deeply appreciated improvement in the pensions of Canadian National employees already retired. I am happy to underline today the appreciation I expressed on that occasion. I refer to the minister's announcement of Friday, February 5, 1971, to be found at page 3102 of Hansard for that date. However, Mr. Speaker, a year has gone by and, as it is popularly put, those concerned are asking, "What have you done for us lately?"
Despite all the good things we were able to say about the announcement of a year ago, we also pointed out then that there were two or three notable shortcomings with respect to what was done at that time. Now we must add to that that one year has gone by, the cost of living has gone up and many CNR pensioners whose position was improved a year ago now find that they are back where they were.
Sir, I said a moment ago that I would confine my remarks tonight to the matter of Canadian National pensions. May I add that I want to divide what I have to say into two main areas. First I want to talk about what can be done to improve further the lot of Canadian National pensioners already retired. Having done that, I shall turn to a second area, namely, the one major improvement, amongst others, that I think ought to be made in the Canadian National pension plan, an improvement affecting those who are still in the service of the CNR.
Going back to my first concern, that of pensioners already retired, may I indicate that the announcement made one year ago was that there was to be provided an increase in the pensions of those who had retired on or before December 31, 1969, and that that increase would amount to 2 per cent for each full year of service. That increase was made effective on January 1, 1971. The pensioners concerned got their first payment of the increase in April of last year, and they have been getting ever since the increase so provided. However, the principal shortcoming of that increase was that it was a one-shot proposal: the increase was granted then, but there was no provision for an additional increase in 1972; there is no provision for another increase in 1973, and so on. Thus, although the cost of living is going up at between 4 and 5 per cent a year-and I think that is a conservative estimate for me to make-these people do not even get the 2 per cent increase in their pensions that quite a number of pensioners under other jurisdictions now receive.
I said on February 5, 1971, that that was one of the main shortcomings in the announcement made at that time. I pointed out that it was a one-shot proposition and that
March 6, 1972

there was no provision' for these increases to be granted on an annual basis. May I point out, Sir, that that is what is done with respect to the pensions of retired public servants. The increases that were provided for them a year or so before that were reasonably comparable to the increases provided for retired Canadian National employees. Actually, they were better, because there was a compounding element in those increases that Canadian National pensioners did not get. Not only did public servants get the first increase; they have continued to get the increase of 2 per cent on the gross amount they are receiving every January as the cost of living has continued to go up. That applies also to those on old age security who are also receiving the guaranteed income supplement.
I regret that it does not apply at present to those receiving only the basic old age security pension. However, it also applies to all sorts of other people who are retired under federal auspices. It applies to retired Members of Parliament, and so on. If any one of us leaves this place and goes on pension he will find that, provided he is over 60, his pension will increase by 2 per cent per year if the cost of living has gone up by that much. History seems to suggest that it will continue to go up by at least that amount.
My point is that- although there are these other groups which not only get pension increases but which also get these increases every year, the increase for Canadian National pensioners was a one-shot proposition and there was nothing after that. I think that is grossly unfair and something ought to be done about it. Not only have there been no subsequent increases for these people; in addition, any employee of Canadian National Railways who retired on or after January 1, 1970, is not covered by the scheme that was announced one year ago. Those Canadian National employees now retiring are retiring on what I regard as the worst kind of pension, namely, a pension of fixed amount with no provision for that amount to be increased.
Sir, this whole matter was discussed at length in the session previous to this one. Indeed, it has been discussed for a great many years. During the third session of the present Parliament we had the matter referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for a very thorough study. That committee made a report, to be found in Journals of the House of Commons for 1969-70 at pages 1290 to 1296. The report was tabled on October 5, 1970, and is found in the pages I have indicated.
I also point out that this report, which was a unanimous report as far as the committee was concerned, became the opinion of this House of Commons because later, as noted at page 1425 of Journals for that same session, that report was concurred in on a motion made on behalf of the committee by the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner). The recommendations of the committee to which I have referred became, as I say, the recommendations of this House of Commons.
As I have indicated, the report covers a number of pages. I am not going to take the time to read them all. I
CNR and Air Canada
am not even going to read all of the seven recommendations with which the report concludes. Instead, I draw particular attention to three of those recommendations. I mention the first one because it is a case where I can extend my compliments to the Canadian National Railways. I am referring to the third recommendation, which was that the Canadian National pension board should be restructured. Its powers should be increased substantially. In particular, we asked for equal representation, as we put it, between the unions and the company. The old set-up was that the board consisted of seven persons, three appointed by the employees through their unions, three appointed by the company and a chairman appointed by the company. That is a strange brand of equality. In effect, it became a seven-man committee with the company having four men on it.
This was responded to rather generously by the Canadian National in that the pension board now consists of ten members; five from the management side and five from the employees side, with the chairmanship alternating. I forget the period of time for which each chairman presides over the committee. At any rate, the chairmanship alternates between a representative of management and a representative of the employees. That is good. In addition, although I do not believe this is written into the rules of the pension board, there is an understanding that each of the two sides will ensure that one of its five representatives is a pensioner so that the viewpoint of those now on pension will have some representation on the board.
The whole question of how much power that board has is another matter. I will not take the time to go into it now. However, I wanted to refer to recommendation No. 3 of our committee which, as I say, called for the restructuring of the pension board as well as for its democratization, and to say that I welcome the action that has been taken. I can also say that many pensioners and employees of Canadian National take heart from this change. They hope that beneficial results will follow from it. The other two recommendations to which I draw special attention are Nos. 4 and 5. I quote No. 4 as follows:
At the outset, this committee wishes to point out that the Canada pension plan and the Quebec pension plan adopted the principle of adjusting pensions for cost of living increases. Furthermore, a second important principle has been adopted whereby Parliament in the name of all Canadians applied the cost of living adjustment ,on a current basis, but more important, retroactively to all public service pensioners.
The committee strongly recommends that these principles be adopted on a broader basis and that other major employers, including Crown corporations, recognize their obligation to follow the lead of Parliament in this regard. The committee specifically recommends that the Canadian National Railways implement these principles forthwith.
Let it be very clear that what we were recommending in that fourth recommendation in our report was that the Canadian National Railways should do what was done by Parliament for public servants and what has been done in the Canada pension plan and the Quebec pension plan, namely, that the escalation of pensions should be put on an annual basis. In other words, every year in which the cost of living goes up, pensions should go up accordingly. There is a 2 per cent ceiling there which I do not like or accept, but that is another issue.

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
Welcome though the announcement of the Minister of Transport on February 5, 1971, may have been, it was only one portion of what the committee recommended. It was only a one-shot increase with no future increases provided. I contend that one of the things that certainly needs to be done is to make it clear to Canadian National that, good as this was a year ago, it is not now good enough. Even if we have to live with this 2 per cent ceiling for a while, until we get rid of it in the Old Age Security Act, the Public Service Superannuation Act and so on, surely we could at least provide the same benefit for Canadian National pensioners who are retired, namely, an escalation of their pensions every year in which the cost of living increases. I believe very strongly that this should be done.
When we get this bill to the committee, I believe the Canadian National officials should be asked to come before the committee and answer the obvious question: When you accepted our recommendation, why did you accept it on only a one-shot basis? Why did you not accept it on the basis which we proposed, namely, that it be an annual increase as is the case with public servants, the Canada pension plan, the Quebec pension plan and so on?
We will have to remind the Canadian National officials when they come before us that because of the motion made later by the hon. member for London East, which had the unanimous support of this House, that recommendation was the recommendation of the House of Commons.
The other recommendation in this report to which I would like to draw attention is No. 5. It is rather lengthy. Perhaps I might be permitted to summarize it, hoping that I will not do violence to it. It is one of those recommendations that gets all-involved in amounts of money owing to the fund, amounts that are paid, amounts that are not paid, interest on those amounts, and all the rest of it. Those on the committee will remember we had long and involved arguments about all this. The company was accused by some witnesses of running away with money and so on.
Even when you boil all this down to a minimum, and even when you deal only with what the committee could support unanimously, we came up with the recommendation that there is an amount of $7 million annually that Canadian National should be putting into the pension fund and that that annual debt of $7 million arises because of what we call in our report the oldest contributions in the fund. We say that this $7 million that is owed annually should be used for the benefit of the oldest employees. I quote:
For these reasons, the pensioners appear to this committee to have a prior claim on any surplus designated by the company.
The committee accordingly recommends that the benefits arising from the allocation of this surplus should be separate from and prior to the cost of living adjustments referred to in paragraph 4.
Now may I try to put that, if I can, into plain language, or at least into language which is plain to me? What we have said is that we think Canadian National pensions should be escalated on an annual basis as is the case with public service pensions. But, we added, before this is
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).)
done, before the annual escalation arrangement is started, there is an annual amount of $7 million which should be used to bring up the low pensions of those who have been retired for many years.
The company may say that it raised the $25 pensioners to $50 a month. But how can one expect anyone to regard $50 a month as a pension on which one can get along at all nowadays? I suggest it bears no relation to what we feel should be done with that $7 million. Therefore, I believe I am expressing the view of the committee when I say that though we are grateful for what was done, not enough was done and we think the Canadian National should review the whole matter.
I have done most of my talking in this whole area about the need to place this escalation on an annual basis. But I also believe that this question of the proper use of that $7 million a year for the benefit of those whose pensions are in the lowest categories needs to be reviewed, and I should have thought that what we asked for needs to be implemented to the full.
These are the views I have in respect to the CNR pensioners already retired. When we talk about pensioners already retired, as far as the announcement of last year is concerned the only people who got any benefit from it were those who retired not later than December 31, 1969. With regard to any who have retired since and are on fixed pensions, they have received no increases. I do not think this is good enough. Of course, if the business before us had to do with the Canadian Pacific I would probably be holding up what the Canadian National had done as an example and saying that the Canadian Pacific had really given its pensioners a lousy deal. That is terribly true. But though it can be argued that the CN arrangement is better than that handed out by the CP, I suggest that the Canadian National arrangement is not good enough for all time. It may have been good enough for the year in which it was announced, but it does not measure up to what was asked for in the report we tabled in October, 1970.
I want to emphasize the importance of this matter and I hope the committee will go at it seriously and with a sense of responsibility. Canadian National pensioners were heartened by the increase a year ago. They have been heartened by the fact that two of their number, one an employee and the other a management type, are now on the pension board. I urge that this sense of progress not be frustrated by nothing further being done. The Minister of Transport said last year that these other matters could be left to collective bargaining. That is not the way to treat persons who have already retired on pensions. It is important that we provide for our Canadian National retired employees at least the same kind of treatment as is provided for retired public servants, retired Members of Parliament and others.
The other area to which I should like to address myself is the question of improving the Canadian National pension plan for those still in the service of the company. Here again, I speak as strongly as I can. When one gets into these pension matters the complications and involvements are many and one can soon get lost in them. But I will stick to one point. I think the time has come when the factor for computing all pensions by the Canadian
March 6, 1972

National should be set at 2 per cent. Not many years ago the plan was so complicated that some service was computed on the basis of 1 per cent, some at 11 per cent and some at 11 per cent.
Over the past decade things have improved until the over-all factor is now 11 per cent. In other words, a CN worker trying to work out what his pension will be has to multiply the number of years of service by 11 per cent, and that total percentage is applied to what might roughly be called his average earnings in his five best years. By the way, in order to get this 11 per cent factor the employees had to accept an increase in the amount they pay toward the plan. First it was 51 per cent, then it was 6 per cent and finally it was raised to 61 per cent. Of course, this is modified to the extent the plan is related to the Canada pension plan. I will not go into that, now; I mention it only so that no hon. member will think I am not aware of this aspect. 1 point out that again this is grossly unfair. Public servants get a pension based on 2 per cent per year of service. A public servant who works 35 years gets a pension of 70 per cent of his salary in the five or six best years of his service. But a CNR employee will get only 521 per cent of his salary during his best five years.
In the case of Members of Parliament, we did a little better for ourselves. Our plan provides 31 per cent for the first ten years, 3 per cent for the next ten years and 2 per cent for the last five years. So we can reach a full pension of 75 per cent in 25 years. A Canadian National employee cannot do that: he cannot work enough to reach that level.

speechtext:
Well, I thought that if I mentioned the MP's plan I would get attention. I did so in order to make a comparison. By what standard of fairness can we say that in our own case we should have the benefit of these higher factors, 3 i per cent and so on, that in the public service the factor should be 2 per cent, and deny these levels to others? How can we say to CNR employees, "The most you can get is 11 per cent for each year of service"?
I shall place another argument before the House in this connection. It is one which has come into the picture only
CNR and Air Canada
recently. I have here a copy of the pension rules for Air Canada dated September 30, 1967, but also, thanks to Air Canada officials, a copy of a statement issued by the management of that company's pension and retirement program from which I learn that on November 1, 1971, a number of changes were made in the Air Canada pension plan, the most significant of these being an increase in this basic factor about which I have been speaking. The result is that as far as Air Canada pensioners are concerned, service is now computed on a 2 per cent basis.
I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that from a technical point of view the CNR owns Air Canada-in the name, it is true, of the people of Canada, but nevertheless that is the technical set-up. So here we have the CNR owning Air Canada, and Air Canada providing its employees with pensions at the rate of 2 per cent for each year of service, while the CNR itself provides pensions for its own employees on the basis of only 11 per cent. I do not see how this can be allowed to continue. I know someone will want to tell me that Air Canada's change was made only recently, and that is correct; it was made effective November 1, 1971. Around this place one does not get overly excited at a delay of a few months. Only when things go on for 10, 20 years does one get excited about delay.
However, I do plead that if just about every other group coming under the aegis of the federal government has a pension arrangement that is based on a 2 per cent factor, then it is a case of gross discrimination and is, indeed, a gross insult to Canadian National employees to say that their pensions must continue to be based on a factor of 11 per cent.
I could go into some of the other details and the combinations that exist between age and years of service. Indeed, I could go into many of the improvements that need to be made in the Canadian National pension plan. I could speak favourably about some of the arrangements for early retirement, though I think they could be greatly improved. But I believe it is the part of wisdom to stick to this one issue which I think is terribly important, namely, that the basis for computing all pensions for those now in the service of Canadian National should be raised from the present 11 per cent to 2 per cent.
So as I said at the outset, I have spoken about two main areas of Canadian National pensions. I am concerned for the well-being of those who are now retired; I am also concerned for the future well-being of those now in service. We can do something really worth while for those who are now retired if we put the escalation of their pensions on an annual basis and if we carry out the recommendation I referred to earlier, namely, seeing to it that those in the lowest pension categories have their pensions brought up to current levels even before we talk about their escalation. For those in service who have their pensions to look forward to, we can do something worth while if we introduce into their pension plan the 2 per cent factor, which is the factor used by Air Canada and by the public service and is pretty generally used by a great many pension plans.
I say again that I was one of those who was happy on February 5, 1971, to welcome the changes that were then

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
made. As all of us said on that occasion-and I think we had the right to say it-one of the reasons that those changes came about was that the committee had pushed very hard for them. The committee had made a unanimous report and that report received unanimous endorsa-tion on the floor of this House.
Therefore, I ask that the members of this House again speak clearly on this issue. The way to do that, of course, is for the committee to consider these matters, have the Canadian National officials before it and bring back a report to this House. When that report comes back, I hope it will call clearly and categorically for an annual escalation of the pensions of those who are retired, and for increasing the basic factor in calculating pensions for those who are still in service to 2 per cent, as I have suggested. If we do these things, the committee will have done a good job, and it is a job we must do.

I hope this will be another great one. However, when one follows the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), particularly on the subject of pensions, about the only thing one has left to say is "Me, too". Because he does a tremendous amount of research work and the points he makes are so well made and presented, I know he will have the support of the House. At least, if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre keeps them honest as far as pensions are concerned, then the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) keeps them honest as far as their work operation is concerned.
I should like to start on a happy note by dealing with Air Canada, followed by what I hope is a hopeful note in regard to the CNR, and then make a very quick conclusion. For four years I have been travelling almost exclusively with Air Canada, and being an incurable voyageur I would have to say that the stewardesses of Air Canada are perhaps the most gorgeous, pleasant and efficient group of stewardesses that I am happy to have had serve me. I hope that, with that comment, all stewardesses will read my remarks and will give me an extra lump of sugar in my coffee next time I travel with that airline.
More seriously, I should like to deal with the circuitous route that we make Canadian National and Canadian Pacific travel when they apply to abandon a service which actually they have no intention of abandoning in order to qualify for a government subsidy. I refer to an application to abandon a passenger service which has as its only aim to secure a subsidy from the government because the particular line is not paying. In most instances, when the CNR makes application to abandon a passenger route the people in the immediate community are up in arms and wonder why the action is being taken. This means that the public relations image of Canadian National-or it may be Canadian Pacific-takes a complete nose-dive.

I believe there are between 35 to 50 applications for abandonment now before the Canadian Transport Commission. In many of these instances, as I say, the railway company in question has no intention of abandoning a stretch of line but has to follow this circuitous route in order to secure a government subsidy. I am sure a minor change to a regulation or section of the act would eliminate this procedure. Not only would the railway company benefit as a result, but they might find that instead of antagonism from the municipalities they hope to serve, those municipalities would assist them.
Let me give an example. In my area we have excellent bus and air services. It is a short distance by road from Sarnia to Toronto and this means the CNR faces a tremendous amount of competition. If CNR simply applied for a subsidy, the citizens of Sarnia might be prepared to assist the company. However, when they apply to abandon a stretch of line, it does raise the hackles not only of the chamber of commerce but of everybody else in the community. As I say, a minor change to a regulation or to the act might eliminate this, to the benefit of the railway company and the communities affected.
Railways are obliged to maintain their services even if they are run at a loss. The managerial decision that must be made is how much loss the railway can afford and still carry on the service on which it is losing money. Where a railway can make a good case for abandonment, I think a second look should be taken at the property rights and privileges granted the company when the line was built in the first place. If the railway company had to surrender a valuable piece of property fronting a river or a lake, then it might take a long, second look at any application to abandon a passenger service before proceeding further.
I also think there is a role to be played by both CN and CP working together, as is the case with CN-CP Telecommunications. I think there is a role to be played in the passenger transportation field where they are not competing with each other but complementing the services provided. I am not going to usurp the role of management, Mr. Speaker, but this is an area they have to look at. Another area is the trans-Canada trains that come to Montreal and Halifax. The same train seems to come all the way across the country and if it has difficulty in the western provinces with weather, a person in central Canada could be left waiting five or ten hours or even a day. I believe that some thought should be given to what might be called a shotgun approach so that if this kind of problem occurred it could be overcome by running several trains and the people would not have to wait for service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues from the Atlantic region, I am unable to allow this bill to pass without saying a few words about the transportation policy in our region, especially in the province of Newfoundland which I represent.
As my colleague from St. John's East has pointed out, Canadian National has most certainly failed in its obligations to the Newfoundland people. I am referring, of course, to the decision made in 1968 and supported and approved by an order of the Canadian Transport Commission which allowed Canadian National Railways to discontinue its rail passenger service in our province. This has been an unpopular decision. I think I might say that as long as Canadian National and the federal government insist on forcing upon the people of Newfoundland a grossly inadequate bus service, members from our prov-' ince will object to the passing of the Canadian National Railways and Air Canada financing bill. And rightly so, Mr. Speaker, because we are reflecting the feelings of the vast majority of people in our province.
Newfoundlanders will not accept the second-class transportation system that has been imposed upon them by Canadian National with, as I say, approval of the CTC. Over the past three years the bus service has proven to be inadequate, unsafe and a very inferior type of ground transportation. This decision is all the more difficult to accept when one remembers that just a few months ago the Canadian Transport Commission refused permission to Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway to discontinue rail passenger service in the Mari-times area. As my colleague from St. John's East pointed out, that service will cost the Canadian taxpayer approximately $12 million a year by way of subsidy, or $1 million a month.
The basis upon which permission to discontinue rail passenger service in Newfoundland was granted was mainly that it was costing too much money to operate and losses were too great. Mr. Speaker, the loss incurred by the rail passenger service in Newfoundland came to less than $1 million a year-less than one-twelfth what it will cost the government to maintain the service in the Mari-times region. I do not want to give the impression that I oppose the CTC decision with respect to the maritime provinces, but I believe that part of Canada is as entitled to a modern, up to date rail passenger service as any other part of Canada. However, it makes it seem worse because we in Newfoundland have to tolerate a grossly inferior, unsafe and unsatisfactory transportation system.
The arguments advanced by the CTC with regard to the application of CPR and CNR to discontinue the Maritimes rail passenger service could be advanced for the reinstatement of the rail passenger service in Newfoundland. My
CNR and Air Canada
colleagues and I have petitioned the Canadian Transport Commission to reopen the case and to allow us to appear before it to advance an argument for reinstatement. Scarcely a day goes by that an editorial or article does not appear in one of the Newfoundland papers dealing with the inadequacy of the so-called road cruiser service. We find that in the past three years there have been more than 40 accidents, some of them very serious. Buses have actually been blown off the highway.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize but I have not been in contact with Newfoundland for the past four or five hours! I appreciate the hon. member correcting me on the number of accidents because this is very important. If it were not so serious it would be laughable to read of buses being lost in a snowstorm with 30 or 40 passengers on board and of buses being blown off the highway.
Early in the winter I had occasion to drive over the trans-Canada highway through part of my riding. I noticed a CNR bus off the side of the road which had just been blown off by a very severe storm. Then I had quite an interesting experience during the recent air controllers' strike. My wife and I had to get back to Ottawa, and the only way to travel was by road cruiser as far as Port aux Basques, then across on the ferry service and then by train to Ottawa. I must say that the bus trip was quite an experience.
The Canadian National have the nicest, the most shiny, most beautiful water-cooler of any bus in Canada. There was only one problem-no water. They have a shiny, chrome-plated dispenser for cups-a credit to them-but no cups. In the toilet there was a lovely, porcelain sink but no water and no plug. This Mr. Speaker is the type of service we are expected to tolerate in our province, a service which would not be tolerated, I submit, in any other province of Canada.
As I say, so long as this land is represented in this House, and so long as Canadian National insists on imposing on the Newfoundland people this secondary and inferior service, Newfoundland members will have to rise in their place to oppose and object to the services and the passing of the Canadian National and Air Canada financing bill. There are a number of problems I could raise in respect of the Canadian National and its operations in our province, but first let me say an argument will be advanced by Canadian National and by others, such as engineers and editorial writers, that in Newfoundland the
574

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
only satisfactory answer would be to have a wide-gauge railway service provided in the province.
Engineers say that with a narrow-gauge railway it is almost impossible to run a smooth and efficient rail passenger service. I cannot think of any better way for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to put its money where its mouth is, as it were, than to provide perhaps a wide-gauge railway service for the province. This is essential for the future development of our province: it is essential in so far as the movement of people is concerned. As a matter of fact, when I think back to 1948 or 1949 when the Terms of Union were being negotiated between Canada and Newfoundland, I sometimes wonder why the Fathers of Confederation, the people charged with responsibility for drafting the terms, did not insist that this be one of the terms of union-that is, that a wide-gauge railway be provided in our province. Certainly, if it is needed now it was needed at that time. This is one thing I believe the people who negotiated the terms will have to answer for in years to come.
Canadian National, as I say, has failed in its obligation to the Newfoundland people. I feel the recent increase in freight rates has already been reflected in an increased cost of living. St. John's, the city I represent with my colleague from St. John's East, has probably the highest cost of living in Canada. It is continuing to rise. I think 4.6 per cent was the figure for last year. Of course, the increase in freight rates will most certainly be reflected in the cost of living index for St. John's.
Then we have the matter of ferry rates. The only line between Newfoundland and the Canadian mainland, unless one travels by air, is by the Port aux Basques-North Sydney ferry service. I contend that this 100 miles of water separating our province from the mainland of Canada should be treated like any other 100-mile stretch of the Trans-Canada highway. I see no reason why people travelling to and from our province should be penalized because Newfoundland is an island. I feel the rates on that ferry should be reduced to a point where they would compare with any 100-mile stretch of the trans-Canada highway. A man, his wife and perhaps three children travelling across the gulf would pay almost $40 for that 100-mile stretch, whereas to travel the same distance on the trans-Canada highway would cost $15.50, or less than $20.
I believe that in Newfoundland, Canadian National is failing in its obligation to the people in that it has not given serious consideration to the potential of the Canadian National dockyard operation in St. John's. St. John's has been referred to by people as the service station of the Atlantic. I feel Canadian National has ignored the potential of the harbour and its facilities, to the detriment of people working at the CN dockyard and to the economy of the city generally. As a matter of fact, its policy in respect of its dockyard operation in St. John's is a very miserly one. If there is a slack period of a month or two or three weeks because ships are not coming in, rather than trying to place the employees in other jobs within its operation the company lays off these men. I feel this is very unfair. I think if the CN were to give more thought to its planning, these lay-offs could be avoided.
fMr. Carter.]
Therefore, I would strongly suggest that Canadian National undertake immediately a study of the potential of its dockyard operation in the harbour. I am quite confident that once such a study was completed a need would be shown for upgrading of the docking facilities in St. John's harbour, to the advantage of the people who work for Canadian National and to the economy of the city generally.
I could speak further on the failings of Canadian National in the Atlantic region and especially in Newfoundland, but I think I have made my point, especially in respect of rail passenger service, the inadequacy of the road cruiser or bus service and the fact that our people are subjected to a grossly inferior, inadequate and unsafe service.
I would strongly recommend and urge the government, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission to pay heed to the submission made in February, at which time we requested an opportunity to meet with the commission and, hopefully, have reopened the case for rail passenger service in our province. I believe that if they are prepared to listen to what we have to say, bearing in mind that we reflect the views and thoughts of the vast majority of Newfoundlanders, something will be done. Certainly, something must be done because I do not think our people, any more than the people in any other Canadian province, deserve to tolerate this type of ground transportation service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again Parliament has been called to its yearly exercise of rubbert-stamping expenditures of the Canadian National Railways and Air Canada for the coming year. Most of this money has already been spent, and it is of deep concern to me that regardless of the amount of money we pour into the hands of these companies we as Members of Parliament are constantly being told of the poor passenger and freight service that CNR and, quite often, Air Canada are providing.
The National Transportation Act of 1967 comes from the Royal Commission on Transportation known as the MacPherson commission. The preamble of the act reads:
-an economic efficient and adequate transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation.
The principle of subsidization for any service that is uneconomical but is required in the public interest is embodied in the legislation. Politicians past and present have, so far as I can find out, assumed that the CTC and the railways were talking of passenger service only. Mr. T. W. G. Macdougal, executive vice-president of the CNR, in a speech to the Canadian Railway Club said:
-at last we are making sense out of the railway passenger business and may, in the near future, begin to make similar progress toward rationalization of the grain gathering and distribution system which is so important to the Canadian economy.
If the same pattern is used in the grain industry that has been used in the passenger service we can well imagine that, in the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), "somebody is going to get hurt". In trying to understand and to make sense out of the practices of the CNR, we
March 6, 1972

consulted the American Everyday Dictionary, the Consolidated Webster Encyclopedia Dictionary and, finally, Colliers Standard Dictionary, international edition, where it says:
The act of bringing an industry into accord with up to date methods of organization and operation-
Even then one must stretch one's imagination to come to grips with the term "rationalization." The CNR has apparently applied this interpretation only in the business sense. The reasoning here was verified by an official appearing on television and saying that they are not really interested in cattle transportation as it is a marginal business, and by an official of the CTC saying that the Canadian railways are much better off because of permissive legislation allowing the railways to diversify, and that in Canada they would never have eliminated 50 per cent of passenger business in one sweep as has happened in the U.S.A.
It would appear that the CNR is diversifying its assets if more profit can be made in some other area. This policy can have no other effect but to force more and more trucks on our highways that are already overloaded. The truth of this can be seen in the poor service provided to cattle shippers this past fall and winter. What has happened here is already a well established and recognizable practice of the downgrading of service until those involved seek other modes of transportation.
If the government is happy with the present operation of the CNR and the CTC, and if we are satisfied with their interpretation of the legislation, then many Canadians are sure that the management should be congratulated because we are sure that according to their ideas they are doing a first-rate job. If you are not, I would suggest that as a first step toward rectifying the situation we put more common sense railway men on the CTC and indicate to that body the kind of railway service which the people of this country want and deserve.
In my opinion, transportation in Canada, especially passenger service, is badly planned. It is provided by many companies on an ad hoc basis, and the general idea is that the public, who in all cases are called upon to pay the bills, are not considered in any way. For example, train 154 arrives at London from Sarnia at 12.45 p.m., and 146 from Windsor at 13.35, so if you are coming from Windsor and wish to go to Stratford or Kitchener you have lost your train connection when you arrive in London. You have two choices, either to remain in London until 20.05 at night or go to Toronto and come back by the other route. For many years these trains met in London, but today the CNR has made changes so that the connections are no longer possible.
I have attempted to show the members of this House some of the results of the short-sighted policies followed by the CNR. Successive federal governments have paid lip service to the need for a rational transportation system in Canada. By "rational" they meant a system in which the basic transportation needs of the population in each region would be supplied by whatever mode of transport was most efficient and economical.
The MacPherson royal commission was supposed to recommend the rationalization of Canada's competing and overlapping transportation service. The new trans-
25020-37 J
CNR and Air Canada
portation act of 1967 was supposed to have enacted policies to reach that objective, and the new Canadian Transport Commission was given a mandate to implement these policies. What do we find today? Our transportation system is in a worse mess than it ever was. How the CTC can pay lip service to rationalization and ignore the need for transportation between Montreal and Ottawa is more than we can understand. One can drive or travel by bus over the worst, most dangerous stretch of the trans-Canada highway, go by rail, by CN, CP or by air: there is no doubt that the fastest, most efficient, most economical and safe method of transportation is fast, up to date rail service.
The more one examines the federal government, the CNR and CPR transportation policies, the more confusing they appear. All the various agencies are pulling at crosspurposes, each launching contradictory projects that have nothing in common except that they all cost the taxpayers millions of dollars. On the one hand we have the CNR, a Crown corporation, systematically trying to scuttle its passenger service with the encouragement of the CTC, and while the CTC is permitting the railways to kill their passenger trains another government branch is paying half the cost of producing a high-speed rail passenger coach.
Meanwhile, the Department of Transport is not satisfied that travel service between Ottawa and Montreal is sufficiently diversified, so the department has extended more subsidies to the Air Industries Association of Canada to provide another mode of transportation between the two cities, that is, the short-landing and take-off aircraft scheduled for operation in 1973. This money would be better spent in upgrading the rail service in Canada.
Canadian citizens who in all cases are called upon to pay the shot find very confusing the continuing insistence that the CNR is in business to provide a service. Not one politician is happy with the CNR and only the CTC and the top officers of the CNR seem satisfied.
The basic idea of the founders of this great country was to unite the east and west and all parts of the expanding country with a rail line for the purpose of transporting people and goods across this nation. Therefore, we can assume that their idea was to create a service industry, and this is the only type of product the CNR has to sell. The CNR was created by the federal government of the day by taking over a group of bankrupt railways. Was the basic idea of the merger to run a railway for a profit or break-even point, or was it to provide a service to the people of Canada? I believe that the provision of service is the answer. Today the CNR has a group of academics and even specialists, and their new ideas are causing undue problems with the employees and shippers across this nation.
Although there are undoubtedly many good recommendations in the MacPherson report, many Canadians consider that the basic philosophy of the report is wrong, that to embrace the free enterprise system and the pursuit of profit to cure the ills is wrong. The CNR came into being for a different reason and should be required to provide service at a reasonable cost. The interpretation of this could be either that all service must perform at a profit or that service should be provided at a reasonable cost to the

March 6, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
taxpayer if necessary. To require the railway to operate on profit alone is to set them apart from all other industry engaged in transportation, such as the trucking industry, air lines, bus transportation and ships. Perhaps the permissive legislation allowing the railway to diversify is wrong if the policy of the CNR is designed to have the company use some other forms of transportation owned by the CNR.
All tax money comes from the same pocket and many people either recognize or ignore this fact. Therefore, we the people of this nation are entitled to and require a modern, up to date railway service for both passengers and freight in addition to other forms of transportation. There is plenty of room for all modes of service and there is no reason why all services cannot be tied into a modern system using the railways as the key link.
I find it refreshing that one of our cabinet ministers has finally come to view the CTC as a rubber-stamp for the railways. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) recently said-
