For that reason he said he would like to see the "public interest" lawyers represent the people-the traveller, the radio listener, the TV viewer, the consumer, at agency hearings of all kinds. The "public interest" lawyer's job would be to appear before an agency and make sure that the views of ordinary citizens who would be affected by its decisions were fully presented.
"Let's take a situation where one of the railways goes before the Canadian Transport Commission to ask for an increase in fares," Mr. Turner said. "At present the railway makes its pitch. Its competitors appear along with the air lines, maybe truckers, certainly boards of trade, sometimes different cities and so on. But surely there ought to be evidence submitted by some one representing the travelling public, the people who pay the shot."
I agree 100 per cent with the minister, Mr. Speaker, and I sincerely believe that he is on the right track. New servo-centres have been established in many key cities in Canada serving large areas of shippers, and after talking to many employees I find that in their opinion this service is not as good as the old system. Stationmasters, station agents and assistants are no longer employed, and thus passengers and freight shippers are robbed of the personal touch.
Service agents and their staff lived in the communities and therefore had a constant dialogue with the shippers. Today this service has been replaced by salesman and their assistants working out of the servo-centre offices. Many employees tell me that the CNR has lost contact with the customers because this new service is not provid-

ing the personal touch which for many years was the key to obtaining business.
Recently a cattle shipper was informed that his cattle shipment would be in the London yard at such a time. Naturally he drove to London to pick up his stock, but due to the fact that the freight service does not run daily to his area, the stock was routed via Stratford and therefore it was waiting for him in Stratford instead of London. This caused the shipper undue delay and extra driving costs. It is my understanding that the company is reassessing its position on servo-centres at St. Catharines, Kitchener and Windsor. If this is true, Mr. Speaker, one would think that perhaps the new system is not doing the job it was set up to do.
I now turn to the question of the morale of the employees of the CNR. In some areas during the past few months the management has begun to do something about the situation and is having a little meaningful dialogue with various groups of workers. Recently meetings were held on the subject of company discipline. Some of the discipline recently handed out by officials has been rather severe. They take the rule book and state that the person involved violated such and such a rule. They do not take into consideration today's length of trains, new triple valves, new brake-shoes and the general idea that no two trains handle alike. Today, Mr. Speaker, a crew can have a short, heavy tonnage train and next trip have a long train with less tonnage.
Many of these officials who are handing out discipline have never had the experience of running a train and therefore do not know what the men are up against. Mr. Speaker, it is one thing to read it out of a book and tell a man how to do his job, but it is a different thing if that same man cannot sit down and show you how to do the job. The employees of the CNR once were a proud group of employees. They were a quite happy group who enjoyed going to work and were sorry to see retirement date appear. Today most employees can hardly wait for retirement date; they are not the same group of happy employees.
I now refer to the pensions of CNR employees and of former employees. About a year ago one change was made and pensioners who were then retired received an increase in their pensions covering the years they had been retired. To me this was very good, but why we did not tie in a 2 per cent increase every year as long as they live is beyond my comprehension. Retired public servants get their 2 per cent increase yearly, and I contend that the pensions of retired CNR and CPR employees, and of the employees of all railways, should be escalated and increased on an annual basis in the same way as the pensions of retired public service employees. The CNR is a Crown corporation and CNR employees are not inferior to civil servants and should be treated in the same way as civil servants.
I believe that employees of the CNR and CPR are entitled to a new deal as far as pensions are concerned. Today, when an employee does not receive sufficient pension on retirement he must seek other employment to provide the additional money required or he must provide a bank account to assist him until the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security program are
March 6, 1972

available to him. It would, therefore, be appropriate if the federal government and, industry, in conjunction with Canadian National pensions and the Canada Pension Plan, were to provide the means and funds for increased pensions so that older employees could take advantage of early retirement. We should do that instead of paying unemployment insurance benefits to the less fortunate; thereby we should be increasing job opportunities for younger graduates coming into the labour force who have found it increasingly difficult to find suitable employment.
It would appear that the CNR management is of the opinion that if the full increase in pension benefits as requested were granted to employees, or if a compulsory retirement age of 60 were provided, the result would be that a large segment of senior supervisory staff would be removed. These supervisors are not irreplaceable. Mr. Speaker, this is a hot issue with the CNR, no doubt it is with the CPR as well as with all railway companies. Employees are requesting that pension benefits be based on 2 per cent of salary per year of service and that the age be reduced to 60. If this cannot be accomplished at once, they should be given a complete financial statement as to the types of investment the pension fund has made. As of December, 1970, the reserve in CNR pension trust funds amounted to $1,160,488,477. There are no moneys out on loan, but investments are made in bonds, mortgages, stocks and short-term investments.
Of the total reserve, only $818,203,051 is represented by investments, cash and accounts receivable. The remainder, $342,283,426 is an unfunded liability, or a bill which the company has to pay. About $299,732,674 is being amortized over a 60-year period and $42,550,752 over a 25-year period, in accordance with the Pension Benefits Standards Act which was passed by the federal Parliament, effective as of October 1, 1967. Mr. Speaker, all Canadians would like a deal like this giving them 60 years and 25 years to pay their debts. Net earnings on investments during 1970 were $23,984,003.
The CNR pension fund supplies each employee with a T-5 slip which states the amount of money he has contributed for the year. For many years during the war they were supplied with nothing. For a time we also received a slip stating the total amount accumulated on our pension account. This has not been done lately. Thousands of employees are pouring money each year into a pension fund and they receive very little information as to the type of investment the money is invested in. Surely the employees are entitled to an annual statement giving them more information than they now receive. If the fund will not generate enough money to lower the pension age to 60, they should be advised of the percentage increase in contributions that would be needed to make the necessary change.
The employees of the CNR, CPR and of all railway companies are patient people who are willing to listen to facts and figures produced by the pensions board. However, if they are not supplied with the necessary information soon on the lowering of the pension age I predict that we will see serious trouble in the railways of this nation. No single issue has grown in importance more rapidly during the past year than that of pensions, largely
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion because of lay-offs and the faster introduction of technological change. All trade unions and their members are making pensions the single, most important issue in collective bargaining.
When a machine is worn out, Mr. Speaker, we replace it with a new one. The workers of all companies in Canada are entitled to a decent pension at an earlier age. They should not be thrown out of work without adequate pensions that are tied to the cost of living. I urge the railways and all industries to update their pension plans and meet the personal needs of employees and retired employees in a fast changing society.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

maintopic: TRADE-DISCUSSION WITH COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN COUNTRIES ON SUGAR TARIFF REBATE
TRADE-DISCUSSION WITH COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN COUNTRIES ON SUGAR TARIFF REBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 25 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) a question concerning the tariff rebate on Commonwealth Caribbean sugar, and I was somewhat surprised at his answer. It was to the effect that the rebate extended to December 31, 1971, had not been cut off at that date. It was my impression that such was not the case and that the rebate had lapsed.
As I have often said before, Mr. Speaker, the abrupt, unilateral termination of this rebate was one of the most regrettable blunders in our dealings with the governments of the Commonwealth Caribbean. The most excellent report of the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs of the Senate of Canada also referred to this matter. Page XVI of the foreword to their report states:
Serious misunderstandings have recently arisen, due in part to the manner in which decisions were unilaterally arrived at.
We recall, too, that the government leader of the Senate made a long, good will tour of the Caribbean area. This was followed by the government's change of heart with the announcement that the rebate which was to terminate on December 31, 1970, would continue until December 31, 1971. This announcement made front-page headlines in the press of the Caribbean countries of the Commonwealth. But prior to that there were comments in the Caribbean press which were far from complimentary to Canada. As the Trinidad Guardian editorialized on December 24, 1970:
It is no use pretending that relations between Canada and the West Indies have not been soured this year by the harsh realities which came to the fore.
Here in Canada, the Globe and Mail said:
Sometimes those closest to us are the ones we understand least. The rule applies to nations as well as individuals.
The cancellation was made at a stroke, without any consultation with the governments involved. It showed a clear lack of under-

March 6, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
standing of the feelings of those nations with whom we are supposed to have a special relationship.
It also noted:
We also buy twice as much sugar from South Africa as we do from all the Caribbean countries.
I can say that this question of heavier purchases from South Africa than from other areas might some day be discussed in the House. But my concern is not to belabor the blunders of the past. Rather must we try to avoid such errors in the future. I am somewhat concerned about the degree of consultation. I wonder if we are not a bit short on consultation but long on confusion. Of course, in some areas of the Caribbean the facts of domestic production make the rebate question somewhat academic, but in other areas it is far from academic. It matters and matters greatly. I hope the parliamentary secretary can bring the House up to date on what is happening. What is contemplated and what is the nature and extent of consultation and discussion?
The Commonwealth Caribbean is an area of great importance to us. Our ties have been close and can and should be closer. We must not through carelessness or casualness fracture a longstanding friendship which has of late been somewhat shaken. These neighbours with parliamentary institutions similar to ours deserve a high priority in our foreign policy consideration. We must not take their friendship for granted. We must be ever alert to opportunities to broaden the base of amity and good will. I express the hope that the blunder of 1970 will not be repeated in 1972 and that we will not through halfhearted lack of negotiation have to send my very good friend, dear old Senator Martin, down to the Caribbean to exculpate the blunders of a most insensitive government, as we did two years ago.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul St. Pierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE-DISCUSSION WITH COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN COUNTRIES ON SUGAR TARIFF REBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that I can assure the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Mac-quarrie) that the value of our friendships in the Caribbean with our fellow Commonwealth members and with others is fully appreciated. I will just briefly review the history of this matter.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) told the House on Friday, February 25, which the hon. member mentioned, that the government has not entered into any discussions concerning a possible extension of tariff rebates on Commonwealth Caribbean sugar. The hon. member will recall that the government decided to terminate the sugar rebates paid to sugar producing countries of the Commonwealth Caribbean at the end of 1969, following the successful negotiation of an international sugar agreement. As a result of representations from the region, an extension of the rebates was agreed for 1970 in order to provide the industry with a longer period to adjust to the new circumstances. An additional extension of one year was made following lengthy consultations which Senator the Hon. Paul Martin had with Commonwealth Caribbean governments during his special mission to the region in late 1970.
Announcing the latest extension in December, 1970, the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated that it was for the year 1971 and that the situation would be reviewed

when the government had considered the report of the tariff board on sugar which it was anticipated would be available early in 1971. This report was received by the government last autumn and was tabled in the House on November 10. The recommendations in that report are under consideration by the government and I can assure hon. members that the views of all those who might be affected by its recommendations, including the governments of the Commonwealth Caribbean, will be carefully considered before decisions are taken on the report.
As far as payments of these rebates are concerned, the amount is based on sugar imports from the Commonwealth Caribbean during the calendar year. At present, final figures for 1971 are not yet available; when they are, the payment for 1971 will be made. The payments for 1970 were made in March, 1971.

maintopic: HEALTH-PROPOSED PAYMENT BY GOVERNMENT OF HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CARE PREMIUMS FOR ALL INDIANS
HEALTH-PROPOSED PAYMENT BY GOVERNMENT OF HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CARE PREMIUMS FOR ALL INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 28 I addressed the following question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) who was unavoidably away from the House:
Is the government considering the problems created as a result of differences in the way hospital and medical care premiums are paid on behalf of the Indian people in various provinces, and is the government considering taking steps to pay the health taxes on behalf of all Indians as is the case in Alberta?
The Prime Minister was so interested in my question that I had to repeat it for his benefit and when he finally came to attention and took note of it he said he would take notice of the question on behalf of the minister. Later, I sent a note to the Minister of National Health and Welfare drawing his attention to the fact that I had asked this question and that I intended to place it on the list of subjects to be discussed at the time of the adjournment, and he thanked me for that note. I would like to discuss this question tonight.
I believe it is recognized by all that the federal government has responsibility for providing health care for the Indian people. What is the situation with respect to the payment of premiums, and of medicare premiums in particular? In 1969, Alberta introduced a medical care insurance plan. As I understand it, the federal government registered all Indians residing in Alberta and paid personal health tax on their behalf. Included were all Indians whose names appeared on band lists regardless of whether they resided on an Indian reserve or not. The federal government has continued to pay the health tax in Alberta on behalf of all Indians as defined in the Indian Act whether they reside on or off a reserve. I understand there is some provision for reimbursement from Indian people who are considered to be self-supporting. How this arrangement is working, I do not know.
What is the situation in other provinces such as the neighbouring province of Saskatchewan? The federal government does not pay the hospitalization or medical care tax on behalf of Indians residing outside an Indian reserve though it makes such payments in respect of
March 6, 1972

Indians residing on a reserve or who have been outside a reserve for less than 12 months.
Two questions arise. The first is this: How can the federal government justify handling this program in such a way in one province and in another way in another province? This is especially so with respect to health programs where standards and quality of service or care are given such high importance.
How the government got into such a mess only the minister can explain, and he will have to do so. Can the minister expect any respect for his programs when the government does this sort of thing? There will be justifiable friction and irritation with the provinces, for one thing. Can the minister expect the Indian people to have any respect for his programs, or for the government, when this is what is being done? In such a delicate area that also involves federal-provincial relations, how does the minister justify treating one province differently from another as a matter of policy?
The second question is: What is the justification for treating off-reserve Indians differently from on-reserve Indians or, for that matter, some self-supporting Indians compared with non self-supporting Indians? Does not the federal government have a responsibility here which it accepted under treaties and through various programs over the years? I think the question must be asked: Is this the first step in a process whereby the government is trying to back out of its commitments and programs?
I think present policy discriminates against those Indians who want to join the urban trek to the cities. It discriminates against Indians who try to help themselves by adjusting to changing conditions. Often enough, people complain of Indians not showing sufficient ambition or initiative. What incentive is there for a person of Indian descent to help himself, if this is the approach that is taken by government in the handling of programs that affect him?
I urge the government to treat Indians in all provinces in the same way. I urge the government to accept its responsibility in this area and to pay premiums for all Indians under the Indian Act regardless whether they are on or off the reserve.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Weatherhead (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
maintopic: HEALTH-PROPOSED PAYMENT BY GOVERNMENT OF HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CARE PREMIUMS FOR ALL INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while there is no statutory or binding authority obligating the federal government to provide free health care to Indians at public expense, the federal government has accepted the moral obligation for more than 100 years of ensuring that no registered Indian suffers from lack of medical attention, either due to inability to pay or inaccessibility to adequate care, particularly if there is no other agency to which he can turn for assistance.
Indians should have the opportunity to achieve standards of health which are comparable to those of the rest of the country, and the federal government has maintained a policy of being willing to assist them through the arrangement for, or the provision of, basic public health services and essential treatment, not necessarily always at public expense.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Prior to the implementation of the two major national health insurance programs-hospital insurance in 1958 and medicare in 1968-there were many Canadians who could not purchase hospital insurance or medical insurance or, at best, could only obtain limited coverage or had to pay an unfairly high premium. It will be recalled that the private insurance industry in that era frequently denied health insurance coverage to Canadians on account of age or previous health, and in some cases, regrettably, even because of racial origin, such as Indians.
Consequently, in both of these Canadian health programs, one of the requirements which each corresponding provincial plan has had to meet in order to receive federal financial support is that the provincial plan had to make available uniform coverage to all eligible residents of the province, including registered Indians. This means in effect that a provincial plan cannot charge a particular group of residents a higher premium or give them less coverage than other residents in similar circumstances.
It is not considered to be a violation of the "uniform terms and conditions" concept when a province waives all or part of a health insurance premium on account of age or limited financial resources of the beneficiary, provided that all residents of the province who meet these requirements are treated equally. Where a province wishes to waive health insurance premiums for its residents who have reached the age of 65, for example, this is permitted as long as all residents of the province are entitled to the same privilege on reaching that age. In point of fact, this is the case in Alberta and Ontario-

maintopic: HEALTH-PROPOSED PAYMENT BY GOVERNMENT OF HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CARE PREMIUMS FOR ALL INDIANS
speechtext: And in Saskatchewan. Come on, get up to date.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
maintopic: HEALTH-PROPOSED PAYMENT BY GOVERNMENT OF HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CARE PREMIUMS FOR ALL INDIANS
speechtext:
-and in both of these provinces the premium for Indians on reaching 65 has been waived as for the other residents.
In a similar way, when a province establishes an intermediate scale of health insurance premiums based on income class, this is permitted under the "uniform terms and conditions" requirement of federal legislation as long as all insurable residents of the province receive the same consideration. Thus, in Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta, which are three provinces with scaled premium subsidies for those residents with limited incomes, the registered Indian who is a resident of one of these provinces receives exactly the same consideration as any other resident of his province on applying for premium assistance.

maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-DEATH OF SANDY LAKE WOMAN FROM MALNUTRITION-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON HEALTH SERVICES IN NORTHERN ONTARIO OR PUBLIC INQUIRY
INDIAN AFFAIRS-DEATH OF SANDY LAKE WOMAN FROM MALNUTRITION-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON HEALTH SERVICES IN NORTHERN ONTARIO OR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last I asked the Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) if he was aware of the tragic plight of Indians on the Sandy Hill reserve, 400 miles north of Kenora. The

March 6, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
minister mentioned a few improvements in the situation but did not answer my question on whether he would agree to initiate a public inquiry into the deplorable condition of health services in the area.
A 50-year old Cree woman died on February 24 en route to hospital by plane. Cause of death was officially given as malnutrition and double pneumonia. I maintain that the true cause of her death was bureaucratic neglect and ineptitude.
This woman was 5 feet 81 inches tall, but at the time of her death she weighed only 85 pounds. The circumstances of her death are a source of great bitterness to others in her community. She had spent ten years in a sanitorium where she was treated for tuberculosis and had part of one lung removed. Her medical history clearly indicated the need for close medical supervision during illness, but she was prevented from getting that attention either in her own community at North Spirit Lake or in a hospital until it was too late. This woman lay ill-severely ill-for several days without medical attention. Proper medication was not available, and so she was given two aspirins by a local, lay dispenser. Twenty-four hours later she was dead.
Fifteen hundred treaty Indians live in three communities on the Sandy Hill Reserve. Two of these communities had only lay dispensers; the third had a nursing staff, all employed by the Department of Health and Welfare. The closest doctor is 300 miles away. Details of the woman's illness had to filter through the lay dispenser to the nurses, and through the nurses to the doctor who was the only person with authority to have the woman sent to a hospital. The procedure took a week, and the woman died.
The coroner's jury made five recommendations: home visits by medical personnel should replace radio contact; all personnel performing medical duties in remote settlements should have nurses aid training; medical personnel in remote communities should be permitted to authorize flights of patients for treatment; additional nurses should be stationed in each isolated community; and, finally, a medical practitioner should be stationed in the Sandy Lake area to treat the 1,500 inhabitants.
To further illustrate the need for better medical services in such areas, let me mention that an influenza epidemic afflicted 350 people in the area from mid-December to mid-January. Nine people died. During the whole period of the epidemic, I am told, the Indians at North Spirit Lake received only one visit from a doctor, and he stayed for only two hours. Field workers from the Ontario Union of Indians had 27 people flown to Red Lake hospital. All were admitted, at a cost to the Union of $2,000. I am told that the bill will be sent to the Minister of Health.
The Indians of the Sandy Hill Reserve have several questions to ask of the Minister of Health. They want to know if the minister intends to implement the recommendations in the coroner's report. They want to know why lay dispensers in their area are white instead of Indian. And they want to know why lay dispensers are permitted to administer antibiotic and narcotic drugs to Indians who have not been seen by doctors.
The minister has told the House that steps are being taken to improve Indian health services. Would the minis-
ter agree to tell the House what these steps are, so that the House and the Canadian people can judge the extent of the government's commitment to improving the life of our native people?
On behalf of these people I must urge that the minister not wait until starvation and disease put an end to the problems of the Sandy Hill Indians and Indians in other remote communities, but that he launch a full public inquiry into health services in the north.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-DEATH OF SANDY LAKE WOMAN FROM MALNUTRITION-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON HEALTH SERVICES IN NORTHERN ONTARIO OR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext:
Medical and public health services in the bush country north of Sioux Lookout have been greatly expanded in the past few years through an extensive program made possible by co-operation between the Department of National Health and Welfare and the University of Toronto which deploys medical consultants, physicians and residents making available the highest possible standards of care. Improved communications have been developed between nursing stations which have been built by the department in the larger communities and the base hospital at Sioux Lookout, and between nursing stations and health stations in the small satellite communities which are staffed by community health aides who work on a part-time basis. The department has an active program for training community health aides, and some of the individuals doing this work are qualified as registered nurses or licensed practical nurses. The community health aide on duty at North Spirit Lake was qualified as a licensed practical nurse.
No medical service, however sophisticated, can prevent deaths during epidemics of influenza. Influenza is an acute infectious disease due to a virus for which there is no known specific treatment. Of importance is the rapidity with which epidemics evolve, placing heavy demands on health personnel who must adapt their activities to render assistance to the greatest number and to those who in their opinion need care the most.
It is the minister's view that the recommendation of the coroner's jury at Sandy Lake to the effect that medical authorities should give consideration to requests for home visits is difficult to reconcile with the facts of the case because the patient's death was being investigated and is being investigated. The patient was visited frequently at home along with many others in the community. The home visits at North Spirit Lake were made by a community health aide who is a licensed practical nurse, and also by a registered nurse who responded to the community health aide's request for assistance. Unfortunately, it is not always possible to predict which persons suffering from influenza will develop complications. The large number of persons who become ill not only increases the problems of surveillance but makes routine evacuation to hospital or to a nursing station impossible.
Complications, however, can be serious, develop suddenly and as a rule require care in hospital. The subject of the coroner's inquest was to be flown to hospital December 23, 1971, the same day her condition suddenly deteriorated as a result of a new complication, but the weather prevented this. Evacuation, unfortunately, was not possible until the next day. The existing procedures for chart-
March 6, 1972

ering aircraft are regarded as satisfactory. They are, of course, subject to the availability of aircraft and to the weather.
I understand that the minister has received a full report on the inquest and the matter of the provision of medical
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
services from the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) in whose riding Sandy Lake is located. I understand he attended the inquest and prepared a long memorandum on the matter for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro).
